bundle.domain: Classic presentation of diabetes — symptoms of hyperglycaemia (osmotic symptoms, catabolic symptoms, and the hyperglycaemic-crisis features that make them urgent)

symptoms.display: Passing large volumes of urine / urinating much more than usual
symptoms.mnemonic: 3Ps/4Ps: P (polyuria). Also 'Toilet' in the sourced Diabetes UK 4Ts. No 5Ps source found.
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is one of the three symptoms ADA names as 'classic symptoms of hyperglycemia'. Its presence changes the TESTING PATHWAY, not just the differential: with a random plasma glucose >=200 mg/dL (>=11.1 mmol/L) it establishes the diagnosis on a single sample, whereas in its absence ADA requires a repeat confirmatory test before diabetes can be diagnosed. Recording it therefore decides whether the patient is diagnosed today or asked to return.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes
symptoms.quote: In the clinical scenario where a person has classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss) or presents with hyperglycemic crisis...
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where a clinician cannot rely on the patient quantifying urine volume, nocturia is the more reliably reported and more discriminating question. Ask 'how many times do you get up at night to pass urine, and is that new?' rather than asking for volumes.

properties.display: Waking at night to pass urine (and is this new?)
properties.whyItMatters: Night-time osmotic diuresis is what separates hyperglycaemic polyuria from daytime urinary frequency caused by urinary tract infection, prostatism or high fluid intake. It changes which test is ordered first — glucose versus urine dipstick for infection — and it is the single element of the Diabetes UK 'Toilet' T that they specify ('going for a wee more often, especially at night').

properties.display: How long has this been going on
properties.whyItMatters: Rate of onset changes urgency and likely type, not just history-taking completeness. Onset over days to a few weeks points to insulin deficiency (IDF: type 1 symptoms 'often develop quickly and can become severe') and warrants same-visit glucose plus ketone assessment; onset over months to years fits type 2 and does not carry the same acute risk.

symptoms.display: Excessive thirst / drinking much more than usual
symptoms.mnemonic: 3Ps/4Ps: P (polydipsia). Also 'Thirsty' in the sourced Diabetes UK 4Ts. No 5Ps source found.
symptoms.whyItMatters: Second of ADA's three named classic symptoms; with a random plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L it removes the need for a confirmatory repeat test. It is also the symptom most likely to be dismissed as normal in a hot climate, so recording it explicitly (rather than leaving it to free text) is what stops the diagnosis being deferred.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes
symptoms.quote: In an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L).
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: In hot climates and in manual-labour populations, ordinary thirst is near-universal and a bare 'thirsty yes/no' field will be useless. The discriminating question is whether drinking relieves it — Diabetes UK's own wording is 'not being able to quench it'. This is my clinical reasoning about field design, not guideline text.

properties.whyItMatters: This is the property that makes the field discriminating rather than universally positive. Thirst relieved by drinking is normal physiology; thirst that persists despite drinking is osmotic. Without this qualifier the symptom cannot change any decision in a tropical setting because nearly everyone will answer yes.

IDF pairs this with thirst in both type 1 and type 2 symptom lists ('Abnormal thirst and dry mouth' / 'Excessive thirst and dry mouth'). It is worth a field because it supports osmotic thirst when the patient has already been drinking heavily and so reports thirst as 'controlled'.

properties.display: How long has this been going on
properties.whyItMatters: Same decision as for polyuria: rapid onset raises suspicion of insulin deficiency and moves ketone testing into the same visit.

symptoms.display: New bedwetting in a child who was previously dry (or unusually heavy nappies in an infant)
symptoms.mnemonic: 'Toilet' in the sourced Diabetes UK 4Ts. Listed by IDF as 'Bedwetting'. No 5Ps/3Ws source found.
symptoms.whyItMatters: This is the highest-yield, most specific field in the whole classic presentation, and the one most often missed. It changes the timeframe of action rather than the differential: a previously dry child who restarts bedwetting needs a glucose test the same day, because roughly half of children with type 1 diabetes are already in DKA at diagnosis. Recording it converts a routine appointment into a same-day assessment.
symptoms.standard: IDF type 1 diabetes symptom list; urgency wording from Diabetes UK type 1 symptoms page; DKA-at-diagnosis frequency from ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 2
symptoms.quote: Children with type 1 diabetes are often diagnosed in the setting of hallmark symptoms of polyuria/polydipsia, and approximately half present with DKA.

dangerSign.action: "If you spot any of these signs, see a doctor for a test immediately" — and for a child or young person, "it's important they are assessed on the same day by a GP, or local hospital if out of hours."

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where same-day laboratory glucose is not available, this should trigger a capillary glucose at the point of contact rather than a referral that the family may not be able to act on. Field design should not assume the referral will happen.

properties.display: Child was reliably dry before this started
properties.whyItMatters: This is the entire diagnostic value of the field. Longstanding primary enuresis is common and non-specific; REGRESSION to bedwetting in a previously dry child is what carries the signal and justifies same-day action. Without this property the field would generate false alarms in every household with an enuretic child.

properties.display: How long since the bedwetting restarted
properties.whyItMatters: Duration determines how much catabolic time has already elapsed and therefore how likely ketoacidosis already is — it changes whether ketones are checked now or the child is booked for routine glucose testing.

symptoms.display: Excessive hunger / eating much more than usual
symptoms.mnemonic: 3Ps/4Ps: P (polyphagia). NOTE: this is the one teaching-mnemonic P that ADA does NOT list among the classic symptoms carrying diagnostic weight.
symptoms.whyItMatters: Its decision value is not diagnostic-criterion value — it is the discriminator against the other causes of wasting. Eating MORE while losing weight points to insulin deficiency (calories lost as glycosuria); eating LESS while losing weight points elsewhere, and in a high-TB/HIV-prevalence setting that distinction changes the whole investigation pathway. Record it for that contrast, and do not let it substitute for weight loss in the ADA criterion.
symptoms.standard: IDF type 1 diabetes symptom list ('Constant hunger'); contrasted against ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 2, which names polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss
symptoms.quote: Abnormal thirst and dry mouth, Sudden weight loss, Frequent urination, Lack of energy, tiredness, Constant hunger, Blurred vision, Bedwetting, DKA (Diabetic ketoacidosis)
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: In food-insecure populations, reduced intake may reflect availability rather than appetite. The field should ask about appetite, not about amount eaten, or it will misclassify.

properties.whyItMatters: This is the only property here that changes anything. Weight loss WITH increased appetite is close to specific for uncontrolled insulin deficiency and supports proceeding straight to glucose testing and likely insulin. Weight loss WITH reduced appetite should redirect towards TB, HIV, malignancy or other chronic infection — a different and, in this setting, more probable pathway. Collecting appetite without tying it to weight direction wastes the field.

symptoms.display: Weight loss the patient did not intend
symptoms.mnemonic: Third of ADA's classic symptoms. 'Thinner' in the sourced Diabetes UK 4Ts. Candidate 'W' of the unsourced 3Ws — recorded here as a symptom, not as a mnemonic letter.
symptoms.whyItMatters: Third of the three symptoms ADA names, so it carries the same consequence as polyuria and polydipsia: with random plasma glucose >=11.1 mmol/L, no confirmatory repeat test is needed. Beyond diagnosis it changes TREATMENT SELECTION — unintentional weight loss with hyperglycaemia indicates catabolic insulin deficiency, which points towards insulin rather than starting an oral agent and reviewing in a month.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026, Section 2: Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes
symptoms.quote: In the absence of classic symptoms of hyperglycemia, repeat testing is required to confirm the diagnosis regardless of the test used.

dangerSign.action: "If you spot any of these signs, see a doctor for a test immediately"; in a child or young person "it's important they are assessed on the same day by a GP, or local hospital if out of hours."

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where there is no working scale, or no previous weight recorded, the field must accept a proxy rather than forcing a blank. Diabetes UK's own wording admits the proxy ('or looking thinner than usual'), and IDF says 'Sudden weight loss'. A tool that only accepts kilograms will silently lose this symptom in exactly the settings where presentation is latest.

options.display: Deliberately dieting or exercising to lose weight

properties.whyItMatters: ADA's criterion is 'unexplained' weight loss. Deliberate dieting explains it and removes its diagnostic weight — recording weight loss without this qualifier would let intentional loss trigger a single-test diagnosis it does not support. This property is what makes the field safe to act on.
Only useful paired with the period below — together they give a rate. Rate is what distinguishes catabolic insulin deficiency from slow drift, and therefore whether ketones are checked today.

Loss over weeks in a young person with osmotic symptoms indicates active catabolism and should trigger same-visit ketone assessment; the same absolute loss over a year does not. Without the period, the amount changes no decision.

properties.display: Clothes, belt or ring noticeably looser (proxy when no scale available)
properties.whyItMatters: Keeps the field answerable where no scale exists, which is the setting where this symptom matters most. Without a proxy the field returns null and the ADA criterion cannot be evaluated at all — the tool would fail closed in precisely the wrong direction.

symptoms.display: Unusual tiredness / lack of energy
symptoms.mnemonic: 'Tired' in the sourced Diabetes UK 4Ts. Candidate 'W' (weakness) of the unsourced 3Ws.
symptoms.whyItMatters: On its own it changes nothing — it is one of the least specific symptoms in medicine. Its value is combinatorial: WHO and IDF both list it among the first noticeable signs, and when it accompanies osmotic symptoms it raises pre-test probability enough to justify testing glucose at this visit rather than deferring. Record it to support the cluster, and do not let it fire anything by itself.
symptoms.standard: WHO Diabetes fact sheet; IDF type 1 and type 2 symptom lists
symptoms.standardVersion: WHO fact sheet last updated 14 November 2024
symptoms.quote: feeling very thirsty; needing to urinate more often than usual; blurred vision; feeling tired; losing weight unintentionally
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: In Uganda and comparable settings, fatigue overlaps almost completely with anaemia, malaria, HIV and TB. This field should be built to prompt testing glucose ALONGSIDE those, never instead of them. This is my clinical reasoning, not WHO or IDF text.

options.display: New — within the last few weeks

properties.whyItMatters: Justified here specifically because new fatigue arriving together with thirst and polyuria in a young person suggests insulin deficiency and moves ketone testing into today's visit, whereas longstanding fatigue does not change urgency at all. Without this split the field is too non-specific to act on.

symptoms.display: Blurred vision
symptoms.mnemonic: Candidate 'W' (visual 'wooliness') of the unsourced 3Ws — I could find NO source for that word in any medical context. Recorded here on WHO/IDF authority as blurred vision.
symptoms.whyItMatters: It changes referral triage. Blurring that fluctuates with glucose is an osmotic refractive change expected to settle with glycaemic control, so it does not warrant urgent ophthalmology; sudden or progressive loss is a different problem needing eye assessment on its own timeline. Recording which pattern it is decides whether the patient joins an eye-clinic queue or is reassessed after control improves.
symptoms.standard: WHO Diabetes fact sheet; IDF type 1 and type 2 symptom lists
symptoms.standardVersion: WHO fact sheet last updated 14 November 2024
symptoms.quote: Excessive thirst and dry mouth, Frequent urination, Lack of energy, tiredness, Slow healing wounds, Recurrent skin infections, Blurred vision, Tingling or numbness in hands and feet
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where ophthalmology access requires travel and cost, distinguishing reversible osmotic blurring from true visual loss prevents both wasted referrals and missed ones.

options.display: Comes and goes / varies day to day

properties.whyItMatters: Directly sets referral urgency. Fluctuating blurring is consistent with reversible osmotic lens change and is managed by controlling glucose; sudden loss is not part of the classic hyperglycaemia picture and needs separate urgent eye assessment. This is the property that stops a routine symptom from hiding an emergency.

Osmotic refractive change is bilateral and symmetrical. Unilateral change points away from hyperglycaemia to a structural or vascular ocular cause, changing the differential and the referral destination.

symptoms.display: Genital itching or thrush
symptoms.mnemonic: Candidate 'P' (pruritus) of the unsourced 5Ps — sourced here as a symptom only, NOT as a mnemonic letter.
symptoms.whyItMatters: It changes the test ordered. Recurrent or treatment-resistant genital candidiasis in an adult should prompt a glucose test rather than another course of antifungal — this is the classic route by which type 2 diabetes is found in someone who reported no osmotic symptoms at all.
symptoms.standard: Diabetes UK type 1 diabetes symptoms page (symptom list beyond the 4Ts); frequency support from a retrospective case series
symptoms.quote: genital itching or thrush, cuts and wounds that take longer to heal, and blurry eyesight
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: In high-HIV-prevalence settings recurrent or resistant candidiasis should prompt HIV testing as well as glucose, not glucose alone. This is my clinical reasoning, not text from any source I retrieved.

properties.display: Recurrent, or not cleared by previous treatment
properties.whyItMatters: A single episode of thrush is common and changes nothing. Recurrence or failure to clear is the specific trigger for glucose testing, so this property is what converts a very common complaint into an actionable one.

Generalised pruritus has a wide differential that in this setting includes scabies, onchocerciasis, HIV and renal or liver disease; it does not point to hyperglycaemia the way genital candidiasis does. Separating the two prevents a broad symptom being read as a diabetes clue.

symptoms.display: Repeated skin infections (boils, abscesses)
symptoms.whyItMatters: Same decision as genital thrush: repeated boils or abscesses in an adult should prompt a glucose test at that visit rather than serial courses of antibiotics. IDF lists it among the presenting features of type 2 diabetes.
symptoms.standard: IDF type 2 diabetes symptom list
symptoms.quote: Excessive thirst and dry mouth, Frequent urination, Lack of energy, tiredness, Slow healing wounds, Recurrent skin infections, Blurred vision, Tingling or numbness in hands and feet

properties.whyItMatters: IDF's wording is 'recurrent'. A single boil is unremarkable and triggers nothing; recurrence is the threshold at which glucose testing is warranted. Recording the symptom without this property would over-trigger.

symptoms.display: Cuts or wounds that take longer than usual to heal
symptoms.mnemonic: Candidate 'P' (poor wound healing) of the unsourced 5Ps and candidate 'W' (wounds) of the unsourced 3Ws — sourced here as a symptom only, NOT as a mnemonic letter.
symptoms.whyItMatters: It changes what happens at THIS visit rather than what is on the differential: a person presenting with a non-healing wound and suspected diabetes needs shoes and socks removed and the wound and feet examined now, not a glucose test and a return appointment. It also signals that hyperglycaemia has probably been present for a long time already.
symptoms.standard: IDF type 2 diabetes symptom list; Diabetes UK type 1 symptoms page
symptoms.quote: Slow healing wounds
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Barefoot walking and delayed presentation make foot wounds both more common and more advanced at first contact. The field should assume the foot has not yet been looked at.

properties.display: Is the wound on the foot or lower leg
properties.whyItMatters: A foot wound carries limb-threat risk that a wound elsewhere does not, and it is what should trigger a formal foot assessment rather than simple wound care. This property routes the patient, so it changes management directly.

properties.display: Features suggesting the wound is infected
properties.whyItMatters: Separates a slowly healing but stable wound from an infected one. I have deliberately NOT attached a dangerSign to this symptom because I could not retrieve a guideline (IWGDF or ADA Section 12) stating the urgency thresholds — this property captures the information a clinician needs while leaving the escalation rule to be set once a proper source is obtained. See 'unverifiable'.

symptoms.display: Tingling or numbness in the hands or feet
symptoms.mnemonic: Candidate 'P' (paraesthesia) of the unsourced 5Ps — sourced here as a symptom only, NOT as a mnemonic letter.
symptoms.whyItMatters: Its presence AT DIAGNOSIS changes the care plan, not the diagnosis: it means complications are already established and the person has probably had undiagnosed hyperglycaemia for years, so the visit must add a foot risk assessment and protective foot-care advice rather than only starting glucose-lowering treatment.
symptoms.standard: IDF type 2 diabetes symptom list
symptoms.quote: Tingling or numbness in hands and feet
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where monofilament testing is unavailable, the patient-reported loss-of-sensation property below is the practical substitute for identifying the at-risk foot.

properties.whyItMatters: A symmetrical stocking or stocking-and-glove distribution fits diabetic polyneuropathy; a single-limb or patchy pattern suggests compression, nerve root or other pathology and should redirect the workup rather than be attributed to diabetes.

properties.display: Reduced or absent feeling (rather than just tingling)
properties.whyItMatters: Loss of protective sensation is what makes a foot vulnerable to unnoticed injury and ulceration, and it is what triggers foot-protection advice and regular inspection. Tingling with intact sensation carries much lower risk. The two are routinely conflated in a single field and should not be.

symptoms.display: Vomiting
symptoms.whyItMatters: It converts a suspected new diagnosis into a suspected emergency. Vomiting alongside osmotic symptoms is a presenting feature of diabetic ketoacidosis, which is present in roughly half of children at diagnosis, and it changes disposition immediately — from outpatient testing to urgent assessment with ketones and blood gases.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
symptoms.quote: Nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain are common in DKA (>50%)

dangerSign.action: "If DKA or HHS is suspected, initial samples should be taken" — urgent assessment including glucose, ketones, electrolytes and blood gases. Do not manage as outpatient gastroenteritis while osmotic symptoms are present.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Vomiting is the point at which oral rehydration will fail and the patient must be moved rather than advised to drink. Where ketone strips are unavailable this symptom, with deep breathing, carries most of the diagnostic weight.

properties.whyItMatters: Decides whether oral rehydration is even an option. Inability to tolerate fluids means dehydration will progress regardless of advice given, and mandates transfer for intravenous access rather than a safety-net-and-review plan.

properties.display: Occurring together with thirst, polyuria or weight loss
properties.whyItMatters: This is what separates DKA from ordinary gastroenteritis, which is far more common. Vomiting alone should not fire a diabetes emergency flag; vomiting on a background of osmotic symptoms should. Building the flag on this pairing is what stops the tool crying wolf on every vomiting patient.

symptoms.display: Abdominal pain
symptoms.whyItMatters: It changes the workup in two directions at once. It is a common feature of DKA itself, but the consensus report warns it may instead signal the condition that PRECIPITATED the DKA — so recording it means the team must both treat the crisis and search for a precipitant such as sepsis or pancreatitis, rather than attributing the pain to the DKA and stopping there.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
symptoms.quote: caution is needed with patients who present with abdominal pain because the symptoms could be either a result of the DKA or an indication of a precipitating cause of DKA

dangerSign.action: "If DKA or HHS is suspected, initial samples should be taken." The consensus report further advises that "Further clinical evaluation is necessary if this complaint is not resolved with the resolution of dehydration and metabolic acidosis."

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: In settings where surgical review is not immediately available, documenting whether the pain is localised at first contact is what allows a later reviewer to detect a missed precipitant.

properties.display: Localised to one area, or generalised
properties.whyItMatters: Localised pain raises the likelihood of a discrete precipitating cause needing its own investigation, which is exactly the error the consensus report warns against missing. Generalised pain is more consistent with the acidosis itself.

properties.display: Occurring together with thirst, polyuria or weight loss
properties.whyItMatters: Abdominal pain is extremely common and non-specific; the flag must depend on the hyperglycaemic context or it will fire constantly and be ignored.

symptoms.display: Drowsiness, confusion or reduced consciousness
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is the feature that most directly determines immediate action: a change in cognitive state is listed among the presenting features of both DKA and HHS, and reduced consciousness additionally raises airway risk, so it changes disposition to emergency care and positioning/airway protection before any glucose-lowering decision is made.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
symptoms.quote: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, vomiting, dehydration, and change in cognitive state

dangerSign.action: "If DKA or HHS is suspected, initial samples should be taken." Emergency assessment. Glucose must be measured immediately — a reduced level of consciousness may equally be hypoglycaemia, which requires the opposite treatment.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: In malaria-endemic and high-HIV-prevalence settings, cerebral malaria, meningitis and hypoglycaemia are important competing causes of altered consciousness and must be considered alongside hyperglycaemic crisis. This is my clinical reasoning; I did not retrieve a source that states it.

properties.whyItMatters: AVPU is the property that sets immediate action — anything below 'alert' means the airway must be protected and the patient cannot be given oral fluids or oral glucose safely. It is recordable without any equipment, which is why it is the right scale here.

properties.display: Has a glucose measurement been taken yet
properties.whyItMatters: Prevents the single most dangerous error at this point: assuming hyperglycaemia in an unconscious person with diabetes when hypoglycaemia is at least as likely and is rapidly fatal if untreated. The field forces the measurement to be recorded before treatment is chosen.

symptoms.display: Deep, sighing or laboured rapid breathing (Kussmaul respiration)
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is the bedside sign that separates ketoacidosis from simple hyperglycaemia, and it does so without any laboratory test — which is what makes it decision-changing where blood gases are unavailable. Its presence means emergency treatment for DKA rather than routine initiation of glucose-lowering therapy.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
symptoms.quote: deep breaths with a fruity odor smell

dangerSign.action: "If DKA or HHS is suspected, initial samples should be taken." Emergency assessment for diabetic ketoacidosis.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where ketone strips and blood gases are unavailable, Kussmaul breathing plus the smell of acetone on the breath is the practical substitute for biochemical confirmation of ketoacidosis, and should be recordable as such rather than requiring a laboratory value.

properties.display: Sweet or fruity (acetone) smell on the breath
properties.whyItMatters: Named in the consensus report's own description of the presentation, and it is available at the bedside with no equipment. Where ketone testing does not exist this property is what allows ketoacidosis to be acted on at all, so it changes treatment directly.

properties.display: Is the patient also short of breath or working hard to breathe
properties.whyItMatters: Distinguishes compensatory acidotic hyperventilation, which is deep but not distressed, from a primary respiratory problem such as pneumonia — a different emergency with different immediate treatment, and a common DKA precipitant that must not be missed.

symptoms.display: Signs of dehydration
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is listed among the shared presenting features of DKA and HHS and it determines the route of fluid replacement — whether oral rehydration is adequate or intravenous access and transfer are required. Recording its severity is what makes that call possible.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS — Hyperglycemic Crises in Adults With Diabetes: A Consensus Report
symptoms.quote: polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, vomiting, dehydration, and change in cognitive state
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: I have deliberately NOT set a dangerSign on this symptom. 'Dehydration' as recorded spans mild to life-threatening, and flagging every instance red would degrade the four crisis flags that are properly sourced. The severity property below carries the information instead. See 'unverifiable'.

options.display: Passing little or no urine despite previous polyuria

properties.whyItMatters: Determines route of rehydration and urgency of transfer. The last option is the most important and the most easily missed: a fall in urine output in someone who was previously polyuric signals that fluid depletion has become severe, and it reverses the expected osmotic picture.

properties.display: How quickly the illness has developed
properties.whyItMatters: The consensus report contrasts DKA, where 'time between initial symptoms and acute presentation may be hours to a few days', with HHS, where 'it may take days or weeks to develop'. That distinction predicts which crisis is present and therefore the expected fluid deficit and monitoring intensity.

mnemonicFindings.expansion: Polydipsia (excessive thirst), Polyuria (frequent urination), Polyphagia (increased appetite)
mnemonicFindings.note: Fetched and read. Consumer/patient-education page (medically reviewed by Kelly Wood, MD; last updated 17 April 2025), NOT a guideline. This is the only P-mnemonic expansion that is consistent across every source I could retrieve. The page explicitly does not mention a 4 Ps, 5 Ps or any Ws version.

Fetched and read. Commercial diabetes-app blog, NOT a guideline or teaching institution. Verbatim: 'Polyuria, Polydipsia, Polyphagia & Polyneuropathy'. Note the 4th P here is polyneuropathy — NOT pruritus and NOT poor wound healing. The page does not mention a 3 Ps or 5 Ps version. This is the only sourced 4th-P expansion I found.

COULD NOT SOURCE. I ran five distinct searches ('5 Ps of diabetes'; '"5 P's" OR "five P's" ... pruritus paresthesia'; '"5Ps" ... poor wound healing'; '5 Ps ... polyuria polydipsia polyphagia pruritus'; 'Ps and Ws' mnemonic) and checked Wikipedia's List of pathology mnemonics, which contains no diabetes symptom mnemonic at all. Every retrieved page stopped at 3 Ps or 4 Ps. I could not source pruritus, paraesthesia or poor wound healing as MNEMONIC LETTERS. Each of those three is separately sourceable as a SYMPTOM (see the symptom list), but that is a different claim. Do not ship a '5 Ps' expansion on my authority — I am reporting absence of evidence, and my training-data recollection is exactly what rule 3 forbids me from substituting here.

COULD NOT SOURCE. Searched '"3 Ws" diabetes mnemonic'; '"3 Ws of diabetes" OR "three Ws of diabetes"'; '"three Ws" ... weight loss weakness wounds'; 'Ps and Ws'. No retrieved page documents a 3 Ws mnemonic for diabetes. The individual candidate words (weight loss, weakness/tiredness, wounds/poor healing) are all well sourced as symptoms, but I found nothing presenting them as a 'W' mnemonic. Separately, 'wooliness/woolliness of vision' returned zero relevant hits in any medical context — I could not source that phrase at all, and would treat it as the least likely of the proposed expansions to be real.

mnemonicFindings.mnemonic: 4 Ts (Diabetes UK) — the sourced mnemonic that occupies the space the '3 Ws' is reaching for
mnemonicFindings.expansion: Toilet — 'going for a wee more often, especially at night'; Thirsty — 'being constantly thirsty and not being able to quench it'; Tired — 'being incredibly tired and having no energy'; Thinner — 'losing weight without trying to, or looking thinner than usual'
mnemonicFindings.note: Fetched and read; quotes verbatim from the page. This is a real, campaign-backed, nationally deployed mnemonic from a national charity (not a clinical guideline body). It is worth flagging because it CARRIES the content the 'Ws' seem to be groping for (weight loss + tiredness) while actually being sourceable, and because it is the only mnemonic I found that comes attached to an explicit urgency instruction rather than just a symptom list. The same page adds, outside the 4Ts: 'genital itching or thrush, cuts and wounds that take longer to heal, and blurry eyesight'.

mnemonicFindings.mnemonic: ADA 'classic symptoms of hyperglycemia' (not a mnemonic — the actual diagnostic wording)
mnemonicFindings.note: Fetched and read. This is the most important finding of task (a): the trio that carries DIAGNOSTIC weight in ADA Standards of Care 2026 is polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss — verbatim 'classic symptoms of hyperglycemia (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, unexplained weight loss)'. It is NOT the teaching 3 Ps: unexplained weight loss replaces polyphagia. A tool built on the 3 Ps will therefore collect the wrong third field for the diagnostic criterion. Also note ADA introduces the list with 'e.g.' — it is exemplary, not a closed set.

unverifiable: MNEMONIC '5 Ps': NOT SOURCED. Five separate searches returned nothing beyond 3 Ps and 4 Ps. I could not find any page expanding a '5 Ps of diabetes'. Do not ship a 5 Ps expansion on my authority.

MNEMONIC '3 Ws': NOT SOURCED. Four separate searches, plus Wikipedia's List of pathology mnemonics (which contains no diabetes symptom mnemonic at all), returned nothing. I could not confirm that this mnemonic exists in any published form.

'Wooliness/woolliness of vision': NOT SOURCED IN ANY MEDICAL CONTEXT. Searching the exact phrase returned only agricultural/food-science results and 'cotton wool spots' (an unrelated retinal sign). Of all the proposed expansions, this is the one I would treat as most likely to be a misremembering.

Pruritus, paraesthesia and poor wound healing are each well sourced as SYMPTOMS (IDF, Diabetes UK, and a case series) but I could source NONE of them as a MNEMONIC LETTER. Those are two different claims and I have kept them separate throughout.

WHO Classification of Diabetes Mellitus (2019): NOT READ. iris.who.int returned HTTP 403 on every attempt (direct bitstream URL, handle URL, and the API bitstream endpoint). Nothing in this output is attributed to that report.

WHO PEN (Package of Essential NCD Interventions, 2020) and WHO HEARTS-D (2020): NOT READ. Both are reachable only through iris.who.int (403) or through mirrors (medbox.org, paho.org) that carry metadata and abstracts only — I confirmed by fetching both mirrors that no document text is present. This is a real gap for the resource-limited-settings brief, because PEN/HEARTS-D is exactly where the low-resource diagnostic and referral thresholds would be defined. The only WHO source I actually read is the Diabetes fact sheet (updated 14 November 2024).

Every 'resourceLimitedNote' in this output is MY clinical reasoning about field design for low-resource settings, not text from any WHO or IDF document. None of it should be presented to clinicians as WHO guidance.

symptoms.display: Numbness or loss of feeling in the feet
symptoms.whyItMatters: Numbness signals large-fibre involvement and possible loss of protective sensation (LOPS). LOPS moves the person into a foot-risk category that changes the surveillance interval and mandates foot inspection at every visit (ADA 12.25), and it means a future ulcer will develop painlessly — so the absence of foot pain can no longer be used as reassurance.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12 (Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care)
symptoms.quote: The involvement of large fibers may cause balance issues (including falls), numbness, and loss of protective sensation (LOPS). LOPS is a risk factor for DFU due to predisposition to unrecognized minor trauma.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where no 10-g monofilament or 128-Hz tuning fork exists, WHO HEARTS-D endorses the light touch (Ipswich) test: touch the tips of the 1st, 3rd and 5th toes of both feet for 1–2 seconds; 'LOPS is likely when light touch is not sensed in ≥2 sites.' ADA 12.24 also accepts the Ipswich touch test in place of the monofilament.

properties.whyItMatters: Symmetric, length-dependent (stocking) numbness is typical diabetic distal symmetric polyneuropathy and is managed in primary care. ADA states that neurology referral, electrophysiology or spinal MRI is 'rarely needed, except in situations where the clinical features are atypical (acute or subacute presentation, non–length dependent, asymmetric, and/or motor involvement)'. So distribution is the field that decides whether this is a routine diabetes finding or a different disease needing investigation.

options.display: Both feet and both hands (glove and stocking)
Patchy / not worst in the toes

properties.whyItMatters: ADA names exactly these features as the exception that justifies neurology referral or further testing; recording them (or their absence) is what prevents both unnecessary referral and a missed alternative diagnosis.

options.display: Came on over days to weeks

properties.whyItMatters: ADA 12.18 requires annual 10-g monofilament testing 'to identify feet at risk for ulceration and amputation'. The result — not the symptom — sets the foot risk category and therefore the review interval (WHO: annual if low risk, 3–6 monthly if moderate, 1–3 monthly if high) and whether therapeutic footwear is indicated (ADA 12.31).

ADA: 'In all people with diabetes and DPN, causes of neuropathy other than diabetes should be considered' — naming alcohol, chemotherapy, vitamin B12 deficiency (especially on long-term metformin), hypothyroidism, kidney disease, malignancy and HIV. WHO HEARTS-D repeats the same list. Whether these were considered decides between investigating and simply treating; HIV and B12 deficiency are the two most consequential in a high-HIV-prevalence, metformin-first setting.

symptoms.display: Burning, tingling or shooting pain in the feet
symptoms.whyItMatters: This is painful distal symmetric polyneuropathy, which ADA 12.21 says to assess and treat, and 12.22 constrains to specific drug classes while explicitly excluding opioids. Recording it starts (or corrects) analgesia; WHO adds that painful peripheral neuropathy is itself a referral criterion where pharmacological management is not available locally.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12
symptoms.quote: The most common early symptoms are induced by the involvement of small fibers and include pain and dysesthesia (unpleasant sensations of burning and tingling).
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO HEARTS-D: 'Refer patients with painful peripheral neuropathy to specialized care for pharmacological management of pain.' Where referral is not possible, ADA 12.22's first-line classes (gabapentinoid, SNRI, tricyclic, sodium-channel blocker) are the sanctioned options and opioids/tramadol are not.

properties.whyItMatters: Discriminates neuropathic from ischaemic leg pain, which sends the patient down a completely different pathway. IDF describes diabetic neuropathy as producing 'nocturnal symmetrical pain in the feet'; by contrast ADA 12.27 characterises the vascular symptom as claudication or 'rest pain relieved with dependency'. Pain that wakes the patient but is not relieved by hanging the leg out of bed is neuropathic; pain relieved by dependency is ischaemic and triggers ankle-brachial index and vascular referral.

ADA 12.22 names gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclics and sodium-channel blockers as initial treatments and states 'Opioids, including tramadol and tapentadol, should not be used for neuropathic pain treatment in diabetes given the potential for adverse events except in rare circumstances.' Capturing what the person is already taking is what allows the tool to prompt a switch off tramadol, or a first-line combination, rather than simply adding another drug.

ADA 12.21 frames the indication for treatment as improving quality of life rather than the presence of pain alone. Functional impact is therefore the trigger to start pharmacotherapy, and it is the outcome to re-measure at review to decide whether to continue, combine or stop.

symptoms.display: Unsteadiness on the feet, or falls
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA attributes balance problems and falls to large-fibre involvement, and WHO lists unsteadiness among the symptoms of peripheral neuropathy. The prescribing consequence is concrete and sourced: WHO states glibenclamide is not recommended in 'people who are at risk of falls'. Recording falls therefore changes which sulfonylurea is used — the single commonest prescribing decision in a low-resource diabetes clinic.
