A confirmed postural drop changes antihypertensive dosing and titration and, per WHO, is grounds for referral for suspected autonomic neuropathy.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12 (Recommendation 12.19)
symptoms.quote: Screening can include asking about orthostatic dizziness, syncope, early satiety, erectile dysfunction, changes in sweating patterns, or dry cracked skin in the extremities. Signs of autonomic neuropathy include orthostatic hypotension, a resting tachycardia, or evidence of peripheral dryness or cracking of skin.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Both confirmatory tests are free: a blood pressure cuff and a pulse count. ADA gives the exact thresholds, so no specialist autonomic testing is needed to act.

properties.whyItMatters: ADA defines orthostatic hypotension numerically as 'a fall in systolic or diastolic blood pressure by >20 mmHg or >10 mmHg, respectively, upon standing without an appropriate increase in heart rate'. The measurement, not the symptom, is what confirms cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy and what justifies reducing or re-timing antihypertensives.

ADA: 'Advanced disease may be associated with resting tachycardia (>100 bpm)'. A resting pulse over 100 alongside a postural drop marks advanced cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy rather than simple dehydration or drug effect.

ADA lists syncope separately from dizziness in its screening questions. Syncope raises the stakes materially — injury and driving safety — and is what tips a person from monitoring into WHO's 'Refer patients with suspected autonomic neuropathy to specialized care.'

symptoms.display: Feeling full quickly, bloating, or vomiting after meals
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA is explicit that gastrointestinal neuropathy is a diagnosis of exclusion: the first action is a drug review (GLP-1 therapies, opioids, metformin) and exclusion of gastric outlet obstruction, not a prokinetic. It also explains otherwise unexplained glycaemic swings, which changes insulin timing rather than insulin dose. IDF makes suspected gastroparesis or persistent vomiting a referral criterion in its own right.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12
symptoms.quote: Gastroparesis should be suspected in individuals with erratic glycemic management or with upper gastrointestinal symptoms without another identified cause. Exclusion of reversible/iatrogenic causes such as medications (e.g., certain GLP-1–based therapies, opioids) or organic causes of gastric outlet obstruction or peptic ulcer disease (endoscopy and/or imaging) is needed before considering a diagnosis of or specialized testing for gastroparesis.

dangerSign.action: WHO HEARTS-D lists 'suspicion of ketoacidosis or HHS' among the criteria for which 'Urgent (same day) referral should occur'. Vomiting must not be attributed to gastroparesis until DKA/HHS has been excluded.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO HEARTS-D's same-day rule is driven by urine ketones and bedside signs (severe dehydration, Kussmaul's respiration, altered consciousness) — no imaging or gastric emptying study is needed to make the urgent decision. Formal gastroparesis diagnosis (scintigraphy, breath test) is a tertiary question that should not delay the drug review.

properties.whyItMatters: This is the property that decides same-day referral versus outpatient work-up. WHO lists urine ketones >2+, suspicion of DKA or HHS, and the signs of acute metabolic deterioration (severe dehydration, Kussmaul's respiration, vomiting, altered level of consciousness) as same-day criteria. Vomiting labelled as gastroparesis while DKA is brewing is the classic fatal miss.

properties.display: On a drug that can cause this
properties.whyItMatters: ADA requires exclusion of reversible/iatrogenic causes, naming GLP-1–based therapies and opioids, before gastroparesis is diagnosed. If one is present, the action is to review that drug — not to investigate the stomach.

IDF names this as its own referral trigger: 'People with suspected gastroparesis and/or persistent vomiting should also be referred.' It also separates a nuisance symptom from one that will cause dehydration and unsafe oral drug absorption.

ADA names erratic glycaemic management as the presentation in which gastroparesis should be suspected. Its presence redirects the response from escalating the insulin dose to changing insulin timing relative to meals.

symptoms.display: Diarrhoea, constipation, or loss of bowel control
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA classes gastrointestinal neuropathy as a diagnosis of exclusion that must first account for metformin and GLP-1 adverse effects — so recording this triggers a drug review rather than an anti-diarrhoeal. Faecal incontinence is named separately by ADA and is the variant that most changes a person's life and their willingness to attend clinic, yet is almost never volunteered unless asked.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12
symptoms.quote: Gastrointestinal neuropathies are a diagnosis of exclusion (including consideration of gastrointestinal adverse effects due to medications such as metformin and/or GLP-1–based therapy). They may involve any portion of the gastrointestinal tract, with manifestations including esophageal dysmotility, gastroparesis, biliary dysfunction, constipation, diarrhea, and fecal incontinence.

properties.whyItMatters: ADA lists constipation, diarrhoea and faecal incontinence as distinct manifestations with different consequences. Faecal incontinence is the one that carries a dignity and skin-integrity burden and is a referral-level problem; constipation alone is usually managed in primary care after a drug review.

properties.display: Taking metformin or a GLP-1 agonist
properties.whyItMatters: ADA requires these drug effects to be considered before diagnosing gastrointestinal neuropathy. A yes changes the first action to a dose review or slower titration, and prevents a reversible drug effect being recorded permanently as an irreversible complication.

symptoms.display: Bladder symptoms (nocturia, urgency, weak stream, incontinence)
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA gives an explicit, actionable trigger: formal evaluation of bladder function for people with incontinence or a palpable bladder. This matters because a chronically distended neurogenic bladder causes recurrent infection and obstructive kidney injury that is reversible if found. Note that nocturia belongs here — ADA lists it as a lower urinary tract symptom of autonomic neuropathy, not as a symptom of kidney disease.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12
symptoms.quote: Lower urinary tract symptoms manifest as urinary incontinence and bladder dysfunction (nocturia, frequent urination, urinary urgency, and weak urinary stream). Evaluation of bladder function should be performed for individuals with diabetes who have recurrent urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, incontinence, or a palpable bladder.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: A palpable bladder is one of ADA's four named triggers and needs only a hand — no urodynamics or ultrasound required to justify acting.

properties.whyItMatters: ADA's own list. Incontinence is singled out because it is one of the four findings that mandates evaluation of bladder function; the others describe the picture but do not by themselves trigger it.

ADA names a palpable bladder as a stand-alone indication for evaluating bladder function. It is the finding that distinguishes retention with overflow — which needs drainage — from an overactive bladder, and the two are treated in opposite directions.

symptoms.display: Recurrent urinary tract infections or pyelonephritis
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA makes recurrent UTI and pyelonephritis explicit triggers for evaluating bladder function. Treating each episode as an isolated infection misses the underlying neurogenic bladder that is causing them, so recording recurrence — rather than the current episode — is what changes management.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12
symptoms.quote: Evaluation of bladder function should be performed for individuals with diabetes who have recurrent urinary tract infections, pyelonephritis, incontinence, or a palpable bladder.

properties.whyItMatters: Turns ADA's word 'recurrent' into something a clinic can act on consistently, so the bladder-function trigger fires on a count rather than on whoever happens to remember the previous visits.

properties.display: Any episode involving the kidney (fever, loin pain, admission)
properties.whyItMatters: ADA lists pyelonephritis separately from recurrent lower UTI as a trigger. Upper-tract involvement raises the priority of finding the structural or neurogenic cause because of the risk of scarring and progressive kidney damage.

symptoms.display: Erectile dysfunction
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA lists erectile dysfunction as one of its named screening questions for autonomic neuropathy (12.19). A positive answer is what prompts the wider autonomic and microvascular assessment — ADA directs that autonomic neuropathy be assessed particularly where other microvascular complications exist — and 12.21 makes treating autonomic symptoms to improve quality of life an explicit recommendation. Presence or absence is the whole of the decision here, which is why this field deliberately carries no sub-properties.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12 (Recommendation 12.19)
symptoms.quote: In men, diabetic autonomic neuropathy may cause erectile dysfunction and/or retrograde ejaculation.

symptoms.display: Sexual difficulty in women (desire, arousal, lubrication, pain)
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA records that female sexual dysfunction is commoner in diabetes and describes its specific presentations. Its practical value is that it stops the autonomic sexual-health question being asked only of men — the same 12.21 recommendation to assess and treat autonomic symptoms applies, and without a field for it the question is simply never asked.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12
symptoms.quote: Female sexual dysfunction occurs more frequently in those with diabetes and presents as decreased sexual desire, increased pain during intercourse, decreased sexual arousal, and inadequate lubrication.

symptoms.display: No longer gets warning symptoms before a hypo
symptoms.whyItMatters: This changes the drug, not just the advice. WHO states glibenclamide is not recommended in people with impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia — a directly actionable switch to gliclazide — and that a higher HbA1c target is appropriate where there is frequent severe hypoglycaemia. Worth noting for the model: ADA is explicit that impaired awareness is NOT the same thing as autonomic neuropathy, so it must not be recorded as evidence of it.
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
symptoms.quote: Glibenclamide is not recommended in: … in patients for whom hypoglycaemia is a concern (people who are at risk of falls, who have impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia, who live alone)
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Glibenclamide is often the cheapest and most available sulfonylurea, so this field carries real weight: WHO's own guidance is that gliclazide is preferred and glibenclamide should be avoided in this group, and that hypoglycaemia risk justifies a relaxed HbA1c target rather than intensification.

properties.whyItMatters: WHO's contraindication is drug-specific. Only by recording which agent the person is actually on can the tool prompt the glibenclamide-to-gliclazide switch, or flag insulin as the driver. Metformin alone does not cause hypoglycaemia, so an unaware patient on metformin only should prompt a search for another cause.

properties.display: Episodes needing someone else's help, last 6 months
properties.whyItMatters: WHO defines severe hypoglycaemia as an episode 'during which the patient is unable to self-treat by ingestion of carbohydrates' and names frequent severe hypoglycaemia as a reason to accept a higher HbA1c target. The count is what justifies deliberately relaxing control rather than pushing it.

WHO lists living alone alongside impaired awareness as a reason to avoid glibenclamide, and separately notes insulin may be unsuitable for people who live alone and depend on others to inject. It changes both the drug choice and whether insulin is realistic.

symptoms.display: Dry, cracked skin on the feet / change in sweating
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA lists this as both a screening question and a physical sign of autonomic neuropathy. Beyond that it is a foot-integrity issue: WHO includes dry cracked skin among diabetic foot symptoms, and cracks are a portal for the infection that ends in amputation. The action is specific — daily emollient but never between the toes.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12 (Recommendation 12.19)
symptoms.quote: Signs of autonomic neuropathy include orthostatic hypotension, a resting tachycardia, or evidence of peripheral dryness or cracking of skin.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO HEARTS-D's counselling is deliverable with any emollient: 'Moisturize your feet but not between your toes… don't moisturize between the toes – that could encourage a fungal infection.'

properties.whyItMatters: A fissure is a break in the skin, not dryness. WHO: 'Disruption of protective skin allows for colonization of subcutaneous tissues by microbes.' That moves the person from foot-care advice into the active foot-problem pathway needing treatment by a trained professional.

symptoms.display: Fungal infection or maceration between the toes
symptoms.whyItMatters: WHO classes interdigital fungal infection as a pre-ulcerative lesion requiring treatment by a trained professional — the same category as callus and ingrown nails. Recording it means it gets antifungal treatment as a limb-preservation step rather than being dismissed as cosmetic, which is the point at which a preventable ulcer pathway is interrupted.
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D, Annex 2 (Prevention, assessment and management of diabetic foot)
symptoms.quote: Pre-ulcerative lesions need to be treated by a trained professional by: removal of callus; protection or draining of blisters; treatment of ingrown and thickened nails; antifungal treatment for fungal infections.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Topical antifungal is cheap and widely available; WHO treats this as primary-care work, not a referral, provided the skin is not broken.

properties.whyItMatters: Determines whether this stays a pre-ulcerative lesion treated locally or becomes a break in the skin — WHO's stated route by which microbes colonise subcutaneous tissue — which puts it on the ulcer and infection pathway.

symptoms.display: Ulcer, sore or wound on the foot
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA makes any open ulceration an urgent referral in its own right, and IDF specifies referral to a multidisciplinary foot clinic because that reduces amputation risk and time to recovery. The ulcer is also the gateway finding for the whole limb pathway: IWGDF reports PAD in about 50% of people with a diabetic foot ulcer, so an ulcer obliges an assessment of perfusion whether or not there are vascular symptoms.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12
symptoms.quote: Individuals with any open ulceration or unexplained swelling, erythema, or increased skin temperature should be referred urgently to a foot care specialist or interprofessional team.

dangerSign.action: 'Individuals with any open ulceration or unexplained swelling, erythema, or increased skin temperature should be referred urgently to a foot care specialist or interprofessional team.' Escalates to same-day acute referral if infected, gangrenous, or with critical limb ischaemia (WHO HEARTS-D).

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO HEARTS-D: 'Patients with a foot ulcer should be referred to a more specialized level for further evaluation if management by a trained professional and the necessary equipment and consumables are not available at the primary care level.' The referral threshold is therefore set by local capability, not by the ulcer alone.

properties.display: How long the ulcer has been present
properties.whyItMatters: Two weeks is a defined threshold, not a rule of thumb: IWGDF defines chronic limb-threatening ischaemia as PAD 'in combination with rest pain, gangrene or foot ulcer of at least 2 weeks duration'. An ulcer at or beyond two weeks in someone with PAD meets that definition and triggers vascular consultation.

properties.display: Bone exposed or probed at the base
properties.whyItMatters: ADA: 'when exhibiting clinical signs of infection or when bone is exposed or probed, appropriate diagnostic measures must be used.' In IWGDF/IDSA terms, bone involvement adds the '(O)' osteomyelitis qualifier, which changes imaging, the need for bone culture and the duration of antibiotic therapy. A blunt sterile probe is the only equipment required.

IWGDF Recommendation 3 requires palpating foot pulses in every person with diabetes and a foot ulcer or gangrene, because PAD is present in roughly half of them and determines whether the ulcer can heal at all. ADA 12.27 makes decreased or absent pedal pulses a stand-alone trigger for ankle-brachial index with toe pressures.

ADA 12.26 requires this history be obtained. It places the person in WHO's highest foot-risk band regardless of anything else found today, which sets assessment every 1–3 months and lifelong specialist surveillance (ADA 12.29) rather than annual review.

symptoms.display: Signs of infection in a foot wound
symptoms.whyItMatters: Infection is the usual final precipitant of amputation, and IWGDF/IDSA gives an explicit bedside grading that decides antibiotic route and whether to hospitalise. The critical caveat that this field exists to counter is ADA's: infection in a neuroischaemic foot progresses fast and the outward signs understate its severity — so a mild-looking foot in a numb, pulseless limb must not be graded on appearance alone.
symptoms.standard: IWGDF/IDSA Guidelines on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Diabetes-related Foot Infections
symptoms.quote: Infected: At least two of these items are present: Local swelling or induration; Erythema > 0.5 but < 2 cm around the wound; Local tenderness or pain; Local increased warmth; Purulent discharge

dangerSign.action: WHO HEARTS-D: 'Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: … infected foot ulcer with or without symptoms of systemic infection; gangrene'. IWGDF/IDSA: 'Consider hospitalising all persons with diabetes and a foot infection who have either a severe foot infection'.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: IWGDF grade 4 (severe) requires ≥2 SIRS criteria, three of which are purely bedside — temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate. A white cell count is not needed to classify a severe infection and act. ADA warns that in a neuroischaemic foot the signs may be out of proportion to the true severity, so a low grade should not override clinical concern.

properties.whyItMatters: IWGDF/IDSA requires at least two of these before a wound is called infected, which is what prevents antibiotics for every ulcer. The erythema options are split deliberately: erythema ≥2 cm from the wound margin lifts the grade from mild (2) to moderate (3), changing the antibiotic route and the referral urgency.

options.display: Redness >0.5 but <2 cm around the wound
Redness extending ≥2 cm from the wound margin

properties.display: Involves tissue deeper than skin and fat (tendon, muscle, joint, bone)
properties.whyItMatters: IWGDF/IDSA grade 3 (moderate) is defined by erythema ≥2 cm and/or involvement of tissue deeper than skin and subcutaneous tissue. Depth alone moves the infection out of the mild category that can be managed with oral antibiotics as an outpatient.

Two or more of these make it IWGDF/IDSA grade 4 — severe — which is the guideline's own trigger to consider hospitalisation and intravenous therapy. All three are measurable with a thermometer and a watch.

properties.display: Features of a more serious infection
properties.whyItMatters: These are IWGDF/IDSA's listed findings suggesting a more serious infection. Crepitus, bullae and necrosis point to a necrotising infection, which ADA calls a surgical emergency needing 'immediate surgical referral for wide incision and drainage' — a different and faster action than antibiotics plus admission.

options.display: New numbness or new localised pain

symptoms.display: Red, hot, swollen foot without an ulcer
symptoms.whyItMatters: In a person with neuropathy this presentation is Charcot neuroarthropathy until proven otherwise, and the action is unusual and time-critical: total non-weight-bearing plus X-ray, not antibiotics. ADA states early diagnosis is 'of paramount importance in preventing deformities and instability that can lead to ulceration and amputation'. A foot walked on for a few more weeks collapses irreversibly.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12
symptoms.quote: Special consideration should be given to individuals with neuropathy who present with a warm, swollen, red foot with or without a history of trauma and without an open ulceration. These individuals require a thorough workup for possible Charcot neuroarthropathy… These individuals require total non–weight-bearing and urgent referral to a foot care specialist for further management.

dangerSign.action: 'These individuals require total non–weight-bearing and urgent referral to a foot care specialist for further management.' WHO HEARTS-D independently lists 'suspicion of acute Charcot arthropathy' and 'unexplained red swollen foot' as warranting urgent referral to acute services.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO HEARTS-D names 'unexplained red swollen foot' as an urgent-referral criterion in its own right, so the referral does not depend on being able to confirm Charcot locally. A plain foot and ankle X-ray is the only investigation ADA requires, and non-weight-bearing can be started immediately at no cost.

properties.display: Is there an open ulcer as well
properties.whyItMatters: This is the discriminator. ADA describes the Charcot presentation specifically as occurring 'without an open ulceration'. If an ulcer is present, infection becomes the leading diagnosis and the person follows the infection pathway; if not, Charcot leads and the answer is offloading and X-ray. The two pathways diverge completely.

properties.display: Loss of protective sensation in this foot
properties.whyItMatters: ADA frames Charcot as a condition of the neuropathic foot. IWGDF/IDSA also lists acute Charcot neuro-arthropathy among the alternative causes of skin inflammation that must be excluded before a wound is graded as infected — so neuropathy status directly changes whether antibiotics are the right answer.

ADA: 'Foot and ankle X-rays should be performed in all individuals presenting with the above clinical findings.' Recording whether the mandated test actually happened is what stops a suspected Charcot foot being discharged undiagnosed.

symptoms.display: Change in the shape of the foot
symptoms.whyItMatters: Deformity is one of WHO's criteria for the moderate foot-risk band, which changes review frequency from annual to 3–6 monthly, and ADA 12.31 makes deformity an indication for specialised therapeutic footwear. A newly collapsed or rocker-bottom shape is a different matter — that is Charcot and follows the urgent pathway.
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D, Annex 2
symptoms.quote: Patients can present with symptoms of peripheral neuropathy and or peripheral artery occlusion, such as: … a change in the shape of feet over time
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO's risk stratification runs on inspection alone — deformity, callus, neuropathy, pulses — so the review interval can be set correctly without any equipment.

properties.whyItMatters: ADA distinguishes what each type demands: bunions and hammertoes may need extra-depth shoes, whereas 'Those with even more significant deformities, as in Charcot joint disease, may require custom-made footwear'. A rocker-bottom or collapsed arch, especially if new, redirects to the urgent Charcot pathway rather than a footwear referral.

WHO treats callus as a pre-ulcerative lesion requiring removal by a trained professional, and as the mechanism by which loading escalates to ulceration. ADA adds that plantar calluses indicate raised plantar pressure and are the trigger for pressure-relieving orthoses. It also warns patients against self-treating calluses.

symptoms.display: Black or dead tissue on the foot or toes
symptoms.whyItMatters: Gangrene appears on WHO's same-day referral list and, with PAD, on IWGDF's urgent vascular consultation criterion. The distinction that changes the action is wet versus dry: ADA calls wet gangrene and necrotising soft tissue infection surgical emergencies needing immediate incision and drainage, whereas dry gangrene without infection follows the urgent revascularisation pathway. IWGDF also warns that delay leads to rapid tissue destruction.
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D
symptoms.quote: Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: … infected foot ulcer with or without symptoms of systemic infection; gangrene; critical limb ischaemia

dangerSign.action: WHO HEARTS-D: 'Urgent (same day) referral'. ADA: 'Necrotizing soft tissue infections and wet gangrene are surgical emergencies and need immediate surgical referral for wide incision and drainage'. IWGDF Rec 14: with PAD and gangrene involving any portion of the foot, 'urgently consult a vascular specialist'.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO places gangrene on the same-day list without requiring any investigation, so transfer should not wait on imaging or vascular studies that are unavailable locally.

properties.whyItMatters: ADA singles out wet gangrene, with necrotising soft tissue infection, as a surgical emergency requiring immediate wide incision and drainage. Dry gangrene without infection is urgent but follows the vascular assessment and revascularisation route. This single property separates 'to theatre now' from 'to the vascular team now'.

IWGDF Recommendation 3 requires pulse palpation in anyone with diabetes and a foot ulcer or gangrene. Absent or weak pulses raise the odds of PAD and, with gangrene, meet IWGDF Recommendation 14's criterion for urgent vascular consultation to time drainage and revascularisation together.

symptoms.display: Leg or calf pain on walking that stops with rest
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA 12.27 makes a history of leg fatigue or claudication a direct trigger for ankle-brachial index with toe pressures and further vascular assessment; IDF escalates severe claudication to vascular surgery referral. The essential counterpart is that a negative answer proves nothing: IWGDF states the diagnosis of PAD and limb-threatening ischaemia is frequently complicated by the absence of classical symptoms because neuropathy removes the pain. This field must never be used to rule PAD out.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes — Section 12 (Recommendation 12.27)
symptoms.quote: Individuals with a history of leg fatigue, claudication, and rest pain relieved with dependency or decreased or absent pedal pulses should be referred for ankle-brachial index with toe pressures and for further vascular assessment as appropriate.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: IWGDF Recommendation 1 requires only a history and pulse palpation at least annually — no Doppler. WHO puts 'symptoms and signs of peripheral vascular disease' on its non-emergency referral list, and IDF accepts pulse palpation alone where a Doppler for the ankle-brachial index is unavailable. ADA also cautions that ankle-brachial indices are 'known to be inaccurate in people with diabetes due to non-compressible vessels', so a normal ABI should not overturn clinical findings.

properties.display: Relieved by stopping and standing still
properties.whyItMatters: Separates true claudication from neuropathic pain, which does not respect exertion. The two lead to opposite investigations — vascular studies versus neuropathy management — so getting this wrong sends the patient down the wrong pathway entirely.

IDF sets its vascular surgery referral threshold at 'severe intermittent claudication'. A recorded distance is what makes that judgement reproducible between clinicians and over time, and a shortening distance is the signal of progression.

options.display: Cannot walk far enough to tell

properties.whyItMatters: ADA 12.27 makes decreased or absent pedal pulses a referral trigger independent of symptoms, which matters precisely because IWGDF says neuropathy masks the symptoms. IWGDF adds that an absent or weak pulse increases the odds of PAD, though a present pulse does not exclude it.

symptoms.display: Foot pain at rest, especially at night
symptoms.whyItMatters: Ischaemic rest pain is a component of IWGDF's definition of chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, and WHO puts critical limb ischaemia on its same-day referral list. IWGDF's evidence is that delay costs limbs: revascularisation delayed beyond two weeks increases the risk of limb loss. This is the vascular symptom that must not be filed as neuropathic night pain.
symptoms.standard: IWGDF/ESVS/SVS Intersocietal Guidelines on Peripheral Artery Disease in People with Diabetes Mellitus and a Foot Ulcer
symptoms.quote: Chronic Limb Threatening Ischaemia: a clinical syndrome defined by the presence of peripheral artery disease in combination with rest pain, gangrene or foot ulcer of at least 2 weeks duration.

dangerSign.action: WHO HEARTS-D lists 'critical limb ischaemia' among the findings for which 'Urgent (same day) referral should occur'. ADA 12.27 requires referral for ankle-brachial index with toe pressures and further vascular assessment.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: The discriminating test costs nothing — ask whether hanging the leg out of bed relieves it. IWGDF also cautions that neuropathy can mask this pain and that autonomic neuropathy can leave an ischaemic foot warm, so a warm, painless foot does not exclude critical ischaemia.

properties.display: Relieved by hanging the leg down
properties.whyItMatters: This is the discriminator ADA itself uses — it specifies 'rest pain relieved with dependency' as the referral trigger. Neuropathic night pain is not relieved by dependency. A yes here means ischaemia and a vascular pathway; a no points back to neuropathy and analgesia.

IWGDF requires pulse palpation as part of the relevant PAD history and examination, and ADA makes absent pulses a stand-alone referral trigger. Rest pain with absent pulses is the combination that meets the chronic limb-threatening ischaemia definition and justifies same-day vascular referral.

symptoms.display: Chest pain or chest discomfort
symptoms.whyItMatters: WHO places symptoms or signs of coronary heart disease on its same-day referral list, and IDF's recommendation is to screen for coronary artery disease whenever the patient has typical or atypical symptoms. In diabetes this is the symptom that most often gets minimised, and the decision it changes — emergency transfer versus outpatient investigation versus nothing — has the widest consequence of any field here.
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D
symptoms.quote: Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: … symptoms/signs of coronary heart disease and stroke

dangerSign.action: WHO HEARTS-D's own wording is 'Urgent (same day) referral' for symptoms or signs of coronary heart disease. Graded red here rather than amber because ongoing chest pain at rest may be an acute coronary syndrome, for which same-day is the floor and not the target.

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: IDF notes the electrocardiograph 'has a poor sensitivity for CAD but may identify a previous unrecognized myocardial infarction' — so a normal ECG must not be used to stand down a same-day referral.

properties.whyItMatters: Separates the emergency from the investigation. Pain present at rest or ongoing now is a possible acute coronary syndrome needing immediate transfer; a stable exertional pattern relieved by rest is angina, which follows IDF's 'screen for CAD' route. Without this property the field can only ever fire one alarm for two very different situations.

A crescendo pattern is what distinguishes unstable from stable disease and therefore emergency transfer from scheduled investigation. Recording change against the patient's own baseline is the only way to detect it in a person whose angina is long-standing.

symptoms.display: Breathlessness on exertion
symptoms.whyItMatters: IDF states plainly that coronary artery disease in diabetes may present atypically, naming sudden dyspnoea, and recommends screening for coronary artery disease when the patient has typical or atypical symptoms. Recording breathlessness therefore triggers a cardiac assessment rather than being attributed to age, weight or anaemia — which is the default in a busy clinic and the reason silent coronary disease in diabetes is found late.
symptoms.standard: IDF Clinical Practice Recommendations for Managing Type 2 Diabetes in Primary Care
symptoms.quote: Most guidelines do not recommend screening for macrovascular complications, unless the patient is symptomatic. The symptoms of coronary artery disease (CAD) may be atypical, such as sudden dyspnea.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: IDF's recommendation is symptom-triggered, so no routine screening test is implied — which is the right posture where cardiac investigation is scarce. No danger sign is attached here deliberately: chronic stable breathlessness firing a same-day alert on every visit would train staff to ignore the alert that matters.

properties.whyItMatters: IDF specifically names 'sudden dyspnea' as the atypical coronary presentation. Sudden or new breathlessness therefore falls under WHO's same-day criterion for symptoms of coronary heart disease, whereas breathlessness of months' standing is a chronic work-up. Onset is what separates the two.

An exertional relationship is what places the symptom in IDF's coronary screening trigger. Breathlessness unrelated to exertion points elsewhere — anaemia, chest infection, kidney disease — and should not consume a scarce cardiac referral.

symptoms.display: Vision has got worse
symptoms.whyItMatters: This is the field that separates the routine screening pathway from an urgent one. WHO places 'recent deterioration of vision' on its same-day referral list and directs that patients reporting vision loss at any visit be referred to an ophthalmologist; IDF and ICO both make unexplained reduced visual acuity a referral criterion regardless of what the retina looks like. The counterpart, which the interface must carry, is that normal vision is no reassurance: ADA states that people with vision-threatening retinopathy may be asymptomatic, so this field can never substitute for scheduled retinal screening.
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D
symptoms.quote: Patients reporting vision loss at any visit and those who have not had a retinal examination in the past two years should be referred to an ophthalmologist.

dangerSign.action: WHO HEARTS-D: 'Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: … recent deterioration of vision.'

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: ICO writes explicitly for low- and intermediate-resource settings and its minimum referral rule needs only a Snellen chart: 'Visual acuity below 6/12 (20/40) or symptomatic vision complaints'. ICO also directs referral where the examination cannot be done at all — 'If visual acuity or retinal examination cannot be obtained at the screening examination: refer to ophthalmologist' — so absence of a fundus camera is itself a reason to refer, not a reason to wait.

properties.whyItMatters: WHO's same-day criterion is 'recent deterioration of vision'. Sudden loss over hours or days meets it; gradual blurring over months, particularly around a change in glucose control, follows the routine referral route. This property is what stops every complaint of blurring consuming a same-day slot.

ICO's minimum referral guideline is acuity below 6/12 (20/40) or a symptomatic complaint. This turns a subjective report into ICO's own referral threshold using a chart that costs almost nothing, and ICO requires acuity be recorded for each eye separately.

properties.display: When the retina was last examined
properties.whyItMatters: WHO makes 'have not had a retinal examination in the past two years' an independent referral trigger, and ADA 12.5 sets the screening interval at 1–2 years only where there is no retinopathy and glycaemia is at goal. Recording the interval is what catches the person whose eyes have simply never been looked at.

symptoms.display: Floaters, spots or cobwebs in the vision
symptoms.whyItMatters: ICO's minimum referral guideline covers this as a 'symptomatic vision complaint', which is a referral criterion in its own right independent of measured acuity. That is the decision it changes: an ophthalmology referral for someone whose acuity chart is still normal. Read the unverifiable list before implementing — none of the guidelines retrieved names floaters specifically or grades them as urgent, so no danger sign is set here.
symptoms.standard: ICO Guidelines for Diabetic Eye Care
symptoms.quote: Minimum referral guidelines are as follows: i. Visual acuity below 6/12 (20/40) or symptomatic vision complaints
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Needs no equipment — it is a question. ICO's referral criterion is met on the symptom alone, which is useful where acuity testing or fundoscopy is not available that day.

properties.whyItMatters: Long-standing stable floaters are common and unrelated to diabetes; a new appearance or sudden increase is a change since the last screen and is what makes this a symptomatic complaint under ICO's referral rule rather than a background finding.

symptoms.display: Passing much less urine, or none
symptoms.whyItMatters: WHO puts anuria on its same-day referral list alongside eGFR under 30. This is the one kidney finding in this domain that is symptom-detectable and time-critical; almost everything else about diabetic kidney disease is found on a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR, not by asking the patient.
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D
symptoms.quote: Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: … anuria or eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2.

dangerSign.action: WHO HEARTS-D: 'Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: … anuria or eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2.'

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO's criterion is met by anuria alone, so the same-day referral does not depend on being able to measure creatinine or calculate eGFR locally.

properties.whyItMatters: WHO's same-day criterion is anuria specifically. Reduced output has many benign explanations, principally poor intake in a hot climate; distinguishing the two is what keeps the same-day referral meaningful rather than routine.

symptoms.display: Swelling of the legs, ankles or face
symptoms.whyItMatters: PROPOSED BUT UNSOURCED — see the unverifiable list. None of the six guidelines retrieved lists oedema as a symptom of diabetic kidney disease; WHO and ADA both state that microvascular complications are clinically silent until far advanced and that kidney disease is found by albuminuria and eGFR. The only decision this field can honestly claim to change is that it prompts measurement of urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR and a search for other causes such as heart failure — and it must never be allowed to imply that its absence excludes kidney disease. Do not ship this row with a danger sign or with fetched status until a clinical reviewer sources it.

RETINOPATHY — the biggest gap. No guideline I retrieved grades sudden visual loss, new floaters, flashes or a curtain across the vision as an ophthalmic EMERGENCY. The strongest sourced statement is WHO's 'recent deterioration of vision' on the same-day list, which is what I used. Search results asserting that sudden vision loss and retinal detachment symptoms need same-day referral came from commercial optometry blogs and a UKMLA revision site, not guidelines, and are deliberately not cited. NICE NG242 (2024) covers only people already under hospital eye services and returned 403. The Royal College of Ophthalmologists 2012 guideline PDF 404'd. A clinical reviewer should source the vitreous haemorrhage / retinal detachment emergency pathway properly before this module goes near a patient — the current output under-calls it.

NEPHROPATHY — oedema and frothy urine could not be sourced as symptoms of diabetic kidney disease from any retrieved guideline. Both ADA and WHO frame diabetic kidney disease as detected by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio and eGFR, with WHO stating microvascular complications are 'typically clinically "silent" until far advanced'. The leg_or_facial_swelling row is marked fetched:false for this reason. Do not present a symptom-based nephropathy screen as if it were guideline-backed.

NOCTURIA — the brief listed nocturia under nephropathy. The guidelines say otherwise: ADA Section 12 places nocturia among lower urinary tract symptoms of autonomic bladder dysfunction ('nocturia, frequent urination, urinary urgency, and weak urinary stream'). It is modelled here under bladder_symptoms in the autonomic group. This is a deliberate correction to the brief, not an oversight.

Genital candidiasis and balanitis could not be sourced from any primary guideline retrieved. The only related content was 'Mycotic genital infections' appearing in the IDF document as an SGLT2-inhibitor adverse effect. Assertions that recurrent balanitis should prompt testing for occult diabetes came from StatPearls and case reports, which are reviews rather than guidelines, and are not cited.

Recurrent skin infections and poor wound healing generally (outside the foot) could not be sourced as guideline-recognised complication symptoms. Only foot-specific wound and infection content was verifiable, from IWGDF/IDSA, ADA Section 12 and WHO Annex 2.

Heart failure symptom screening (orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle oedema) is not covered. It sits in ADA Section 10, which could not be retrieved. The exertional_dyspnoea field is therefore scoped to coronary disease only and does not attempt a heart failure pathway.

Silent myocardial ischaemia attributable to cardiac autonomic neuropathy is a widely held clinical belief but was NOT found in any retrieved document. ADA Section 12's cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy passage does not mention silent ischaemia. IWGDF's masking statement concerns limb pain and PAD, not cardiac pain, and has not been extended beyond that here.

The 2023 ESC Guidelines on cardiovascular disease in patients with diabetes were partially fetched from academic.oup.com but the fetch returned only the front matter and table of contents; sections 6.2.1 and 10.1.1 were truncated and never actually read. Nothing is cited from ESC.

Severity mapping of dangerSign is my own judgement, not the guidelines'. Every 'action' string quotes the guideline's own words, but red versus amber is an interface decision. Note in particular: chest_pain is graded red although WHO's literal wording is 'Urgent (same day) referral' (which maps to amber), because ongoing rest pain may be an acute coronary syndrome. Conversely red_hot_swollen_foot and foot_rest_pain are graded amber although both risk limb loss. A clinician should sign off this mapping explicitly.

Symptom property option sets (walking distances, acuity bands, drug lists) are operationalisations of guideline wording, not verbatim guideline categories, except where stated. Sourced thresholds actually taken verbatim: 6/12 (20/40) acuity from ICO; erythema 0.5 cm and 2 cm from IWGDF/IDSA; SIRS criteria of temperature >38/<36 degrees C, pulse >90, respiratory rate >20 from IWGDF/IDSA; postural fall >20 mmHg systolic / >10 mmHg diastolic and resting tachycardia >100 bpm from ADA; ulcer duration of 2 weeks from the IWGDF chronic limb-threatening ischaemia definition. Distances in the claudication field and episode counts elsewhere are NOT from any guideline.

The 5Ps and 3Ws mnemonics were outside this domain (they describe the classic osmotic presentation, not complications) and were not researched. The mnemonicFindings field is deliberately omitted rather than filled with guesses; nothing about those mnemonics should be inferred from this output.

Coverage gap by design: this domain excludes the acute hyperglycaemic crises (DKA, HHS) and acute hypoglycaemia as primary subjects. They appear only where a chronic-complication symptom must not be misattributed — vomiting must not be labelled gastroparesis while DKA is possible (WHO), and impaired hypoglycaemia awareness changes sulfonylurea choice (WHO). A separate domain should cover the crises properly.

The safety counterpart is verbatim ADA: 'people with vision-threatening retinopathy may be asymptomatic', correctly preventing the field being used as a substitute for scheduled screening.
audit.correction: No correction required.

audit.reason: The source is genuine and correctly titled — the PDF's first page reads 'ICO Guidelines for Diabetic Eye Care Updated 2017' — and the quoted criterion exists verbatim under section 2.2: 'Minimum referral guidelines are as follows: i. Visual acuity below 6/12 (20/40) or symptomatic vision complaints'. But the symptom itself is absent: I searched the full 40-page extraction and the words 'floater' and 'cobweb' do not appear anywhere, and every occurrence of 'spots' is either 'cotton-wool spots' (a retinal sign seen by the examiner, not a patient symptom) or 'laser spots'. Classifying floaters as a 'symptomatic vision complaint' is the proposer's inference, not ICO's statement. Mitigating: the proposer disclosed this explicitly and correctly set no danger sign.
audit.correction: Keep the field but restate the provenance honestly: ICO's generic 'symptomatic vision complaints' referral criterion is the source, and ICO does not name floaters. If a floaters-specific citation is wanted, note that ADA Section 12 names 'vitreous hemorrhage and tractional retinal detachment' among ocular complications but does not describe floaters as their symptom, so a vitreoretinal source outside this set would be needed. Do not upgrade to a danger sign without one.

audit.reason: WHO same-day list verbatim: 'anuria or eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2'. The danger quote is accurate and the guideline itself places it in the urgent tier, so the danger sign is earned. The observation that this is the only symptom-detectable, time-critical kidney finding is fair — WHO's other renal criteria (eGFR 30-59, moderately and severely increased albuminuria) are laboratory-based and sit on the non-emergency referral list, which I confirmed.
audit.correction: Scope: WHO lists ANURIA only. The field label 'Passing much less urine, or none' extends the trigger to oliguria, which appears in WHO only as one component of a different bullet ('blood pressure >180/>110 mmHg with headache, shortness of breath, blurred vision, changed mental state, nausea, vomiting, reduced urine output'). Bind the amber danger to the 'degree' property = anuria, and treat lesser reduction as a prompt to measure eGFR/uACR and blood pressure rather than as a same-day referral.

audit.reason: Independently verified and the proposer's self-assessment is accurate. Searching WHO HEARTS-D and ADA Section 12 for oedema/edema returns only diabetic MACULAR oedema (an eye finding) and, in the IDF drug table, 'Edema and bone fracture' as a thiazolidinedione adverse effect. No retrieved guideline lists peripheral or facial oedema as a symptom of diabetic kidney disease. Correctly marked fetched:false with an empty sourceUrl rather than padded with a plausible-looking citation, and correctly carries no danger sign and no properties.
audit.correction: Handling is already correct — do not ship pending clinical review. If later sourced, the honest framing is the one already written (prompts uACR/eGFR and a search for other causes such as heart failure, and never excludes kidney disease by its absence). The pioglitazone/TZD oedema adverse effect noted in the IDF drug table is a legitimate drug-review angle if the row is revived.

Searching all six documents for candid/mycotic/balanitis/thrush returns a single hit: the IDF drug-comparison table listing 'Mycotic genital infections, fractures, amputations' as SGLT2-inhibitor adverse effects. No guideline in this set describes genital candidiasis as a presenting or complicating feature of diabetes. Correctly declared unsourced with fetched:false, no danger sign and no properties.
