bundle.domain: Diabetes — danger signs that mandate urgent action (DKA/HHS, level 3 hypoglycaemia, foot emergencies, sight and vascular emergencies), with the resource-limited referral tier taken from WHO

symptoms.display: Vomiting
symptoms.whyItMatters: Decides whether this is a sick day managed where the patient is, or a hyperglycaemic crisis that leaves for hospital now. Vomiting is present in over half of DKA presentations, and it separately removes oral rehydration as an option, so the patient needs an IV line before transport rather than sick-day fluids.

dangerSign.action: Refer to hospital all patients with suspected DKA or HHS. (DKA or HHS should be suspected in every ill patient with hyperglycaemia.)

properties.display: Able to keep oral fluids down
properties.whyItMatters: WHO HEARTS-D warns that hyperglycaemia slows gastric emptying and oral rehydration might not be effective even in patients who are not vomiting; a patient who cannot hold fluids is one who needs intravenous saline started before the journey.

WHO HEARTS-D makes urine ketones >2+ an urgent same-day referral criterion in its own right, and PEN-H sets referral at blood ketones >1.0 mmol/L. The ketone result is what separates a vomiting illness from ketoacidosis when the glucose alone is equivocal.

properties.display: How long the patient has been unwell
properties.whyItMatters: The consensus report separates DKA (hours to a few days) from HHS (days to weeks). The two differ in the degree of fluid deficit and are resuscitated differently, so the time course changes the fluid plan.

symptoms.quote: Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain are common in DKA (>50%) but are uncommon in HHS.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: The red flag here is conditional on hyperglycaemia, exactly as WHO words it: DKA or HHS is to be suspected in every ill patient with hyperglycaemia. Vomiting with a normal glucose is not a diabetes emergency. Where no ketone strips exist, PEN-H's rule is to check ketones whenever blood sugar is above 14 mmol/L, and if strips are absent the decision falls back on the clinical picture.

symptoms.display: Abdominal pain
symptoms.whyItMatters: In a person with hyperglycaemia it triggers the DKA pathway, and it separately decides whether to hunt for a precipitant: the consensus report warns the pain may be caused by the ketoacidosis or may be the surgical or infective cause of it, and those lead to opposite management.

dangerSign.action: Refer to hospital all patients with suspected DKA or HHS. (DKA or HHS should be suspected in every ill patient with hyperglycaemia.)

properties.display: Pain persists once fluids and insulin have been started
properties.whyItMatters: Pain that does not settle as the ketoacidosis is corrected points to the separate precipitating cause the consensus report cautions about, and switches the plan from treating DKA to investigating the abdomen.

Infection is the most common precipitating factor for DKA worldwide (14-58% of cases in the consensus report); fever alongside abdominal pain adds a source hunt and antimicrobials to the plan rather than fluids and insulin alone.

symptoms.quote: Caution is needed with patients who present with abdominal pain because the symptoms could be either a result of the DKA or an indication of a precipitating cause of DKA.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Red only in the presence of hyperglycaemia, per WHO's own conditional wording. Abdominal pain with a normal glucose in a person with diabetes is not on this list.

symptoms.display: Deep, heavy, laboured breathing
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is the bedside marker of the metabolic acidosis, so it moves a hyperglycaemic patient from same-day review to immediate transfer. Where blood gases are unavailable it is often the only available measure of how severe the acidosis is.

dangerSign.action: Diabetic ketoacidosis is an emergency and requires urgent transfer to hospital.

properties.whyItMatters: The consensus report ties the fruity acetone smell to the same acidosis as the breathing pattern. Where there are no ketone strips it is corroborating evidence for ketoacidosis rather than another cause of tachypnoea such as pneumonia.
PEN-H triages against a stated normal adult range of 12-20/min; a rate outside it is one of the ABCDE findings that places the patient in the treat-immediately-and-refer-immediately group.

symptoms.quote: The respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis found in DKA is manifest by Kussmaul breathing, which consists of deep breaths with a fruity odour smell because of the presence of acetone.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: WHO HEARTS-D words this as 'Severe cases of DKA can present with Kussmaul's breathing' — its presence marks severity, its absence does not exclude DKA. PEN-H's ABCDE triage relies on this sign plus conscious level to identify DKA as one of eight emergency NCD conditions needing treatment within minutes when no laboratory is available.

symptoms.display: Drowsiness, confusion or reduced consciousness
symptoms.whyItMatters: It decides both which emergency this is and what level of care is needed. The same presentation is hypoglycaemia (give glucose) or a hyperglycaemic crisis (fluids and insulin), so it forces an immediate glucose reading; and the consensus report assigns care by mental status, with stupor or coma indicating ICU-level care.

dangerSign.action: Refer to hospital all patients with suspected DKA or HHS. (DKA or HHS should be suspected in every ill patient with hyperglycaemia.)

properties.whyItMatters: PEN-H's ABCDE triage records exactly these four levels, and the consensus report assigns the care setting by mental status: alert to a regular or observation unit, alert-to-drowsy to intermediate care, stupor or coma to ICU.

PEN-H requires a blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis before anything else. Without it the clinician cannot tell which of two opposite treatments to give, and giving the wrong one is harmful.

ADA lists seizure among the outcomes level 3 hypoglycaemia can progress to, and PEN-H lists seizures in its hypoglycaemia column; a fit shifts the immediate action toward glucose and airway protection.

symptoms.quote: Patients with HHS typically present with altered consciousness (stupor or coma).
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
symptoms.standardVersion: 2020 (WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1); management protocol stated to be derived from WHO-PEN 2013
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: PEN-H's worked triage example is exactly this: 'If a person with a history of diabetes has impaired consciousness and fever, diabetic ketoacidosis with sepsis need to be excluded.' Where no glucometer is available this symptom cannot be safely triaged at all and the patient should travel.

symptoms.display: Dehydration — dry mouth and tongue, reduced skin turgor, dizzy on standing
symptoms.whyItMatters: Volume depletion is the first thing corrected and it governs transport. WHO HEARTS-D calls correction of dehydration the critical first step for transport, so recording it decides whether an IV line and saline go in before the patient is moved rather than on arrival.

dangerSign.action: Correction of dehydration is the critical first step for transport. Hyperglycaemia slows gastric emptying, and oral rehydration might not be effective even in patients who are not vomiting.

properties.display: Dizzy on standing, or low blood pressure
properties.whyItMatters: PEN-H records that patients with diabetic ketoacidosis are usually severely volume depleted with orthostatic hypotension; it marks the depletion as severe enough that oral fluids alone will not do.

options.display: Passing normally or passing large volumes

properties.whyItMatters: WHO HEARTS-D makes anuria an urgent same-day referral criterion in its own right. Falling output in a patient who was polyuric marks the switch from ongoing osmotic diuresis to established acute kidney injury, which changes the fluid plan and the urgency.

symptoms.quote: Both conditions may present with polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, vomiting, dehydration and change in cognitive state.
symptoms.standard: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: This is the one danger sign whose action is a treatment that must start at the primary-care level before referral, not merely a referral. WHO HEARTS-D specifies isotonic saline is infused and continued until the patient reaches a hospital; PEN-H gives interim measures when referral is not feasible. Polyuria and thirst alone, without dehydration or intercurrent illness, are poor control rather than an emergency and are deliberately not flagged here.

symptoms.display: Rapid weight loss with thirst and passing large volumes of urine
symptoms.whyItMatters: In someone newly presenting this is the signal for type 1 diabetes, which WHO makes an urgent same-day referral. Starting metformin or a sulfonylurea instead of insulin is precisely how a newly diagnosed type 1 patient arrives back in DKA days later — a common presentation where type 1 is under-recognised.

dangerSign.action: Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: ... clinical suspicion of type 1 diabetes in newly diagnosed patient

properties.whyItMatters: WHO HEARTS-D escalates urine ketones >2+ to same-day referral and PEN-H sets referral at blood ketones >1.0 mmol/L. Ketones in a newly presenting patient means insulin today, not an oral agent, and turns this amber into a red.

PEN-H's type 1 recognition criterion is rapid loss of weight with increased appetite. Losing weight while eating more separates catabolic insulin deficiency from weight loss caused by TB, HIV or malignancy, which is the main competing diagnosis in this setting.

properties.display: Over what period the weight was lost
properties.whyItMatters: PEN-H's criterion is rapid loss specifically. Rapid catabolism over days to weeks is what makes this same-day; the same total weight lost over a year is not.

symptoms.quote: clinical suspicion of type 1 diabetes in newly diagnosed patient
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: PEN-H's supporting type 1 features (age of onset below 50 years, BMI below 25, personal or family history of autoimmune disease) are recorded elsewhere as history rather than as symptom properties. PEN-H also notes that ensuring access to insulin for type 1 patients is a matter of urgency in humanitarian settings, which is why this is a same-day referral rather than a routine one.

symptoms.display: Low blood glucose needing another person's help (level 3)
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is treated in the room immediately, and it changes the treatment plan afterwards: ADA classes it as an urgent medical issue, and it is the trigger for cutting the insulin or sulfonylurea dose, relaxing the glucose target, and prescribing glucagon.

dangerSign.action: Recurrent level 2 hypoglycemia and/or level 3 hypoglycemia is an urgent medical issue.

properties.whyItMatters: WHO HEARTS-D gives oral carbohydrate to a patient who can ingest food or drink and intravenous hypertonic glucose to one who is unconscious or unable to ingest. This property is what picks the route, and getting it wrong risks aspiration.
WHO HEARTS-D makes hypoglycaemia unresolved by treatment an urgent same-day referral criterion. A patient who does not wake up needs to leave the health centre rather than be re-dosed.

properties.display: Number of episodes needing help in the last month
properties.whyItMatters: ADA calls recurrent level 2 or level 3 hypoglycaemia an urgent medical issue, and PEN-H lists recurrent hypoglycaemia as a referral criterion. The count, not the single event, is what forces the regimen and the glucose target to change.

properties.display: Had warning symptoms (sweating, hunger, palpitations, tremor) before the episode
properties.whyItMatters: ADA recommends referring people with impaired hypoglycaemia awareness to trained professionals for intervention to re-establish symptom awareness; absent warning symptoms change the glucose target upward and make continuous or more frequent monitoring necessary.

symptoms.quote: A severe event characterized by altered mental and/or physical status requiring assistance for treatment of hypoglycemia
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 6: Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia
symptoms.standardVersion: 2024 (Diabetes Care 47(Suppl. 1):S111-S125). NOTE: the 2026 edition renames this section 'Glycemic Goals, Hypoglycemia, and Hyperglycemic Crises' — I could not retrieve the 2026 text.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: PEN-H warns that after treatment 'hypoglycemia may recur', so the episode is not closed when the patient wakes and monitoring must continue. WHO HEARTS-D's own threshold for managing hypoglycaemia even without symptoms is a plasma glucose at or below 3.9 mmol/L (70 mg/dL); its threshold for intravenous glucose in an unconscious patient is at or below 2.8 mmol/L (50 mg/dL). No dose is recorded in this field by design.

symptoms.display: Open ulcer, blister or wound on the foot
symptoms.whyItMatters: Any break in the skin below the ankle converts routine foot care into urgent specialist referral. ADA makes any open ulceration an urgent referral and WHO refers on the presence of the ulcer alone, because delay at this point is what turns an ulcer into an amputation.

dangerSign.action: Individuals with any open ulceration or unexplained swelling, erythema, or increased skin temperature should be referred urgently to a foot care specialist or interprofessional team.

properties.display: Signs of infection at the wound
properties.whyItMatters: IWGDF diagnoses foot infection by the presence of at least two of these clinical signs of inflammation, or by purulent secretions. Infection is what escalates an ulcer from wound care to antibiotics and a possible surgical procedure, so the count matters, not the impression.

options.display: Bone visible or touched with a sterile probe

properties.whyItMatters: IWGDF makes osteomyelitis likely when a positive probe-to-bone test is combined with abnormalities on plain X-ray. This changes antibiotic duration and raises the surgical question, and it is one of the few discriminating tests available without imaging.

IWGDF's SINBAD ischaemia item turns on whether at least one pedal pulse is palpable, and WHO HEARTS-D refers to a higher level of care if the pulse is absent, because an ischaemic ulcer will not heal on wound care alone and needs a vascular assessment.

properties.display: How long the ulcer has been present
properties.whyItMatters: IWGDF says an ulcer failing to show signs of healing within 4-6 weeks despite optimal management should prompt angiography and revascularisation, irrespective of the vascular test results. Duration is therefore a referral trigger in its own right.

symptoms.quote: Individuals with any open ulceration or unexplained swelling, erythema, or increased skin temperature should be referred urgently to a foot care specialist or interprofessional team.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12: Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care
symptoms.standardVersion: 2024 (Diabetes Care 47(Suppl. 1):S231-S243). The identical sentence appears in the 2026 edition per search results, but I could not fetch the 2026 text to confirm.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: PEN-H directs primary-level staff to start antibiotic treatment for a suspected diabetic foot infection as soon as possible and, if feasible, take cultures and samples before starting, then refer to hospital — treatment is not held for the referral. WHO HEARTS-D's own primary-care flowchart is simply: examine feet for ulcers at every visit, refer to a higher level of care if an ulcer is present.

symptoms.display: Spreading foot infection, gangrene, or a foot infection with fever or feeling systemically unwell
symptoms.whyItMatters: This is the limb- and life-threatening end of the foot spectrum and it changes the destination and the drug route: IWGDF calls foot infection an immediate threat to the affected foot and limb, and this picture means admission for parenteral antibiotics and urgent surgical assessment, not outpatient dressings.

dangerSign.action: Urgent referral to acute services is recommended for patients with any of the following: infected ulcer; spreading infection; critical limb ischaemia; gangrene; suspicion of acute Charcot arthropathy; unexplained red swollen foot.

properties.whyItMatters: IWGDF grades an infection as severe when it is accompanied by systemic signs of sepsis. Severe infection is what mandates empiric parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent evaluation for surgery rather than oral therapy.

properties.display: Depth and spread of the infection

options.display: Deeper than skin, or more extensive cellulitis, with or without abscess (moderate)
Accompanied by systemic signs of sepsis (severe)

properties.whyItMatters: This is the IWGDF/IDSA mild-moderate-severe grading. Moderate or severe (deep or extensive, potentially limb-threatening) infection is the trigger for urgent evaluation for immediate surgery to remove necrotic tissue, release compartment pressure and drain abscesses.

WHO HEARTS-D names gangrene as its own urgent same-day referral criterion and PEN-H lists it among the acute complications requiring referral; it is one of the findings that removes any discretion about referral.

properties.display: Blood glucose has become harder to control
properties.whyItMatters: IWGDF teaches people with foot ulcers to recognise and report new or worsening infection by, among other things, worsening hyperglycaemia. In a neuropathic foot where pain is blunted, deteriorating control may be the only warning that the infection is advancing.

symptoms.quote: Infection of the foot in a person with diabetes presents an immediate threat to the affected foot and limb.
symptoms.standard: IWGDF Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: IWGDF explicitly warns that the local signs of infection may be blunted by neuropathy or ischaemia and that systemic findings such as pain, fever and leucocytosis are often absent in mild and moderate infections — so a normal temperature must not downgrade this. WHO HEARTS-D's primary-care wording covers the infected foot ulcer 'with or without symptoms of systemic infection'.

symptoms.display: Warm, red, swollen foot with no open ulcer
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is the presentation of acute Charcot neuro-osteoarthropathy, and recording it changes what happens in the room rather than only where the patient goes: the foot must come off weight-bearing immediately, because continuing to walk on it produces the permanent deformity that later ulcerates and costs the limb.

dangerSign.action: These individuals require total non-weight-bearing and urgent referral to a foot care specialist for further management.

properties.display: Open ulcer present on the same foot
properties.whyItMatters: ADA describes the Charcot workup specifically for a warm, swollen, red foot without an open ulceration. An ulcer moves the leading diagnosis to infection, which is a different and more urgent pathway with a different first action.

A cold, pulseless foot points to critical limb ischaemia rather than Charcot, which WHO HEARTS-D handles as its own urgent referral criterion and which goes to a vascular rather than a foot-care service.

symptoms.quote: In any person with diabetes mellitus and with a red, hot, swollen foot, the diagnosis of active CNO should be considered.
symptoms.standard: IWGDF Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: ADA states the presentation occurs 'with or without a history of trauma', so a history of injury neither confirms nor excludes it — it is deliberately not asked as a property here. Where advanced imaging is impossible, IWGDF says the person should be treated as having probable active Charcot, so the absence of MRI is not a reason to withhold offloading. WHO HEARTS-D lists 'unexplained red swollen foot' alongside 'suspicion of acute Charcot arthropathy' as urgent referrals, which is the wording to use where the diagnosis cannot be confirmed.

symptoms.display: Cold, pale or pulseless foot, or pain in the foot at rest
symptoms.whyItMatters: It decides whether the limb needs vascular assessment now. WHO HEARTS-D makes critical limb ischaemia an urgent same-day referral, and IWGDF is explicit that an ischaemic foot will not heal without restoring perfusion, so continuing wound care alone is the wrong plan and loses the limb.

dangerSign.action: Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: ... critical limb ischaemia

properties.display: Pain in the foot at rest, especially at night
properties.whyItMatters: IWGDF warns that symptoms may be absent because of the neuropathy despite severe pedal ischaemia. Pain present raises suspicion sharply; pain absent must not reassure, and that asymmetry is the whole reason for asking.

IWGDF states that peripheral artery disease is less likely in the presence of triphasic or biphasic pedal Doppler waveforms. The finding decides whether to go on to ankle and toe pressures and vascular imaging or to stop.

IWGDF sets urgent vascular imaging and consideration of revascularisation at an ABI below 0.4 or an ankle pressure below 50 mmHg, so this number carries the referral threshold itself rather than merely describing severity.

symptoms.quote: In a person with either an ankle pressure <50mm Hg or an ABI <0.4 consider urgent vascular imaging, always with detailed visualization of below-the knee and pedal arteries, and revascularisation.
symptoms.standard: IWGDF Practical guidelines on the prevention and management of diabetes-related foot disease
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where Doppler and pressure measurement are unavailable, WHO HEARTS-D falls back to palpation alone and refers to a higher level of care if the pulse is absent; PEN-H's high-risk foot criterion is simply 'limb ischemia (weak or absent peripheral pulse)'. The ABI property should be optional and its absence must not block the referral.

symptoms.display: Vision has got worse recently
symptoms.whyItMatters: Recent change, not blurring in itself, is what WHO makes a same-day referral. It separates the person who may have a treatable sight-threatening event happening now from the person who belongs in the routine biennial retinal screening queue.

dangerSign.action: Urgent (same day) referral should occur if one of the following is detected: ... recent deterioration of vision

properties.whyItMatters: WHO's criterion is specifically 'recent deterioration of vision', so recency is the discriminator the guideline itself uses to make this same-day rather than routine. A gradual change over months goes to screening, not to the same-day list.

properties.display: Visual acuity in the worse eye
properties.whyItMatters: ICO's minimum referral guideline is visual acuity below 6/12 (20/40) or symptomatic vision complaints, and it separately says to refer to an ophthalmologist if visual acuity or the retinal examination cannot be obtained at screening — so 'cannot be measured' is itself a referral, not a blank.

symptoms.quote: recent deterioration of vision
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: IMPORTANT SOURCING CAVEAT: the same-day urgency here comes from WHO HEARTS-D, not from ADA or ICO. ADA Standards of Care Section 12 (2024), which I read in full, contains no recommendation specific to sudden visual loss — its retinopathy referrals are graded by retinal findings, not by symptom onset. ICO 2017 says only that 'persons with unexplained visual-acuity loss should be referred' and sets no emergency timeframe. Do not attribute an emergency vision-loss rule to ADA or ICO.

symptoms.display: Chest pain
symptoms.whyItMatters: It puts a person with diabetes straight into the acute coronary syndrome pathway. WHO HEARTS-D lists symptoms and signs of coronary heart disease among the diabetes protocol's own same-day referral criteria, and PEN-H classes acute coronary syndrome as one of about eight emergency NCD conditions needing treatment within minutes.

dangerSign.action: Treat immediately and refer immediately. ... Emergency conditions need immediate treatment within minutes.

properties.whyItMatters: PEN-H's triage table pairs chest pain with exactly these findings as the picture of acute coronary syndrome, and its worked example is that a patient with severe chest pain who is breathless is likely to have one. The combination is what moves the patient into the immediate-treatment group rather than the queue.

symptoms.quote: symptoms/signs of coronary heart disease and stroke
symptoms.standard: WHO HEARTS-D: Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes (referral criterion); PEN-H triage (emergency classification)
symptoms.standardVersion: WHO HEARTS-D 2020 (WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1); PEN-H, International Rescue Committee, year not stated in the document
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Recorded as red rather than amber because although WHO HEARTS-D files it under 'urgent (same day) referral', PEN-H separately classifies acute coronary syndrome as an emergency NCD condition requiring immediate treatment and immediate referral. Where the two differ I have followed the more urgent, and named both sources.

symptoms.display: Sudden weakness of one side of the body, or difficulty speaking
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is the stroke presentation, which PEN-H classes as an emergency NCD condition to treat and refer immediately and WHO HEARTS-D lists among the diabetes protocol's same-day referrals. It also changes handling before transfer, because an unconscious patient may have secretions obstructing the airway.

dangerSign.action: Treat immediately and refer immediately. ... Emergency conditions need immediate treatment within minutes.

options.display: Weakness or paralysis of arm or leg

properties.whyItMatters: PEN-H's ABCDE triage records disability as weakness of face, arms or legs, or paralysis. Altered consciousness in addition raises airway obstruction by secretions, which changes positioning and how the patient is transported.

PEN-H's stroke flowchart requires blood glucose to exclude hypoglycaemia or diabetic ketoacidosis. Hypoglycaemia can produce an identical focal picture and is reversed by glucose given now, so the reading changes the immediate treatment, not just the destination.

symptoms.quote: Weakness or paralysis of limbs
symptoms.standard: PEN-H Package of Essential Non-communicable Diseases Interventions for Humanitarian Settings (triage table); WHO HEARTS-D (referral criterion)
symptoms.standardVersion: PEN-H, International Rescue Committee, year not stated in the document; WHO HEARTS-D 2020 (WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1)
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Red rather than amber for the same reason as chest pain: WHO HEARTS-D files stroke signs under same-day referral, but PEN-H classifies stroke as an emergency NCD condition requiring immediate treatment and referral. PEN-H notes these emergencies are often detected too late in humanitarian settings because health workers are not trained to look for them proactively — which is the case for putting them on a diabetes symptom form at all.

mnemonicFindings.note: Outside this domain (danger signs) I made one search for a 5Ps diabetes mnemonic and found nothing in any guideline or retrievable teaching source. I did not fetch a document defining it, so I am recording nothing. Separately, and this I did verify by reading it: the ADA/EASD/JBDS 2024 hyperglycaemic crises consensus report and WHO HEARTS-D both list DKA/HHS symptoms as prose, and neither uses a 5Ps or 3Ws mnemonic anywhere.

No guideline or retrieved document I read contains a 3Ws diabetes mnemonic. A web search surfaced only the classic '3Ps' (polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia) on flashcard and encyclopedia sites, which I did not fetch and which are not guidelines. Treat both mnemonics as unsourced until a teaching-tradition source is actually retrieved.

unverifiable: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026 (Sections 6 and 12) could NOT be fetched. diabetesjournals.org returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch, to curl with a browser user-agent, and through a text-extraction proxy. Every ADA item above is sourced to the 2024 edition, which I did retrieve and read in full: Section 6 via PubMed Central (PMC10725808) and Section 12 as a PDF hosted at aens.us. Recommendation numbers and wording may differ in 2025/2026 and must be re-checked before clinical release.

Specifically unverified: the 2026 renumbering of the glucagon recommendation (6.16, grade A) and the 2026 hypoglycaemia-awareness screening recommendation (6.11) came only from a Guideline Central secondary summary page, which I did fetch but which is not the ADA text. The 2024 numbers I did read in the ADA-derived document are 6.13 (glucagon, grade E) and 6.16 (refer for impaired awareness, grade A) — note the number 6.16 means different things in the two editions, which is exactly why the 2026 text needs re-fetching.

The verbatim ADA Section 12 foot sentence quoted above was read in the 2024 edition. A search snippet indicated the identical sentence survives in the 2026 edition, but I could not open the 2026 page to confirm it, so treat the 2026 attribution as unverified.

The 2024 hyperglycaemic crises consensus report was read through the PubMed Central full text (PMC11343900), and the quotes came back through WebFetch's summarisation of that page rather than from a file I extracted myself, unlike the WHO, IWGDF and ADA-Section-12 quotes which I extracted from the PDFs directly. The consensus quotes are therefore one step less certain than the others; the primary Diabetes Care copy (diabetesjournals.org, dci240032.pdf) returned 403.

I did not verify the exact DKA and HHS biochemical diagnostic thresholds from the consensus report to a standard I would ship. A fetch returned beta-hydroxybutyrate >=3.0 mmol/L, anion gap >12 mmol/L, glucose >=11.1 mmol/L for DKA and glucose >=13.9 mmol/L with pH >=7.30 and bicarbonate >=18 mmol/L for HHS, but partly as paraphrase. No numeric diagnostic threshold from that report is asserted in the fields above. WHO HEARTS-D's own primary-care-measurable thresholds (DKA plasma glucose >=13.9 mmol/L with positive urine ketones; HHS >=33.3 mmol/L with negative or weakly positive ketones) I did read verbatim and are safer to use at this tier.

WHO PEN itself (the 2020 Package of Essential Noncommunicable Disease Interventions) could NOT be fetched — knowledge-action-portal.com returned 403. The resource-limited referral list captured verbatim above is from WHO HEARTS-D 'Diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes' (Geneva: WHO, 2020; WHO/UCN/NCD/20.1), whose management protocol the document itself labels 'Derived from WHO-PEN 2013'. It is WHO, and it is the right tier, but it is not literally the WHO PEN package document, and the PEN package may word its diabetes referral list differently.

PEN-H is NOT a WHO publication. The document states it was prepared by Shanthi Mendis (former WHO Senior Adviser for NCDs) for the International Rescue Committee with USAID funding. It carries no publication year I could find in the file. It is authoritative for humanitarian settings and its diabetes protocols mirror WHO PEN, but it should be cited as IRC/PEN-H, not as WHO.

ICO Guidelines for Diabetic Eye Care were read from a copy hosted at vrsp.org.ph, not from icoph.org. The file is titled 'ICO Guidelines for Diabetic Eye Care Updated 2017'. I could not confirm from icoph.org that 2017 is still the current edition.

No guideline I retrieved states that sudden visual loss in diabetes is an emergency requiring same-hour ophthalmology review. ADA Section 12 (2024) has no sudden-vision-loss recommendation at all; ICO's referral criteria are not time-graded. The amber same-day rating rests entirely on WHO HEARTS-D's phrase 'recent deterioration of vision'. If a stronger claim is needed, a retinal-detachment or vitreous-haemorrhage source must be fetched first — I did not fetch one, and no such mechanism is asserted above.

I did not source anything on hyperglycaemic crisis in pregnancy, in children or adolescents, or in people on dialysis. The consensus report and ADA Section 14 (children) were not read for those populations, and the danger-sign thresholds above may not transfer to them.

I did not source sick-day rules as an operable rule set. The consensus report states that 'sick day advice' must be provided or reinforced and that each patient must review when to call for assistance, but I did not retrieve a document giving the actual thresholds (how often to test, what ketone level triggers a call). Do not build a sick-day module from this pass.

SGLT2-inhibitor-associated euglycaemic DKA is real and sourced (approximately 10% of DKA presents euglycaemic; the consensus says SGLT2 inhibitors should be stopped on admission), but I have NOT modelled it as a symptom field because it is a medication interaction rather than a symptom. It matters for this list because a normal or near-normal glucose does not exclude DKA in someone on an SGLT2 inhibitor, which would defeat the 'conditional on hyperglycaemia' logic several red flags above rely on. This needs handling in the therapy model before release.

Severity mapping is my own judgement applied to each guideline's own words, not a grading any guideline publishes. I mapped 'emergency', 'urgent transfer to hospital', 'immediate treatment within minutes' and 'refer to hospital' to red, and 'urgent (same day) referral' and 'urgent referral' to amber. Where WHO HEARTS-D and PEN-H disagreed (chest pain, stroke signs) I followed the more urgent and named both sources in the field. A clinician should re-review this mapping.

Anuria was folded into the dehydration field as a urine-output property rather than given its own danger-sign field. WHO HEARTS-D lists 'anuria or eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2' as a standalone urgent same-day referral criterion, so if the eGFR arm is wanted it needs a separate field this pass does not provide.

Two candidates were deliberately EXCLUDED as not meeting rule 5 despite being clinically real: (a) impaired hypoglycaemia awareness — ADA mandates referral but not same-day, so it is a property of the hypoglycaemia field rather than a danger sign; (b) polyuria and polydipsia alone without dehydration or intercurrent illness — no guideline I read makes these urgent on their own, and flagging them would fire on most poorly-controlled patients and destroy the list's credibility.
