bundle.domain: Diabetes mellitus — how hyperglycaemia and complication symptoms should be CHARACTERISED (onset, pattern, precipitants), and which pertinent NEGATIVES change a decision. Sourced for a decision-support tool used internationally, including resource-limited settings.

symptoms.display: Polyuria (passing large volumes of urine)
symptoms.whyItMatters: Presence of classic osmotic symptoms is what licenses a diagnosis from a SINGLE random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L). Without them, a second abnormal test is required before anyone is labelled diabetic for life.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 2 (Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes)
symptoms.quote: In an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L)
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where only one glucose measurement is affordable, the presence or absence of this symptom decides whether that single test can stand as a diagnosis or whether the patient must be recalled. This field carries real cost consequences.

properties.display: Large volumes each time, or frequent small voids?
properties.whyItMatters: Polyuria is a urine output exceeding 3 L per 24 h; frequent small voids is urinary frequency, which points to infection or bladder/prostate disease. Only the large-volume answer supports osmotic diuresis and therefore the symptomatic single-test diagnosis rule.

properties.display: New nocturia, or bed-wetting in a previously dry child
properties.whyItMatters: Waking to pass urine, or a previously dry child wetting the bed, is the 'Toilet' feature of the Diabetes UK 4 Ts and is the pattern least explained by daytime drinking habits or heat. It is the nocturnal-pattern question that actually changes whether you test glucose today.

properties.display: How quickly did it come on?
properties.whyItMatters: Abrupt onset with weight loss and ketosis is among the features ADA calls most useful for identifying type 1 diabetes, and selects the insulin-now pathway. It also separates the two crises: DKA develops over hours to a few days, HHS over days to weeks.

properties.display: How long have the symptoms been present?
properties.whyItMatters: Recorded because ADA names duration of symptoms before presentation as a type 1 vs type 2 discriminator — but explicitly a LESS discriminatory one. Capture it, weight it weakly, and never let it alone decide the type.

symptoms.display: Polydipsia (excessive thirst)
symptoms.whyItMatters: Second member of the classic triad that licenses single-test diagnosis; and whether the patient can still drink enough to replace osmotic losses decides between oral rehydration and immediate intravenous fluids.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 2
symptoms.quote: classic hyperglycemic symptoms (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss)

properties.whyItMatters: 'Being really thirsty and not being able to quench the thirst' is the Diabetes UK wording; it separates osmotic thirst from ordinary thirst in a hot climate or after work.

properties.display: Can the patient keep fluids down?

options.display: Vomiting or unable to keep fluids down

properties.whyItMatters: Both DKA and HHS present with vomiting, dehydration and change in cognitive state. A patient who can no longer replace what they are losing needs intravenous fluids and transfer, not advice to drink more.

symptoms.display: Polyphagia (excessive hunger)
symptoms.whyItMatters: Eating more while losing weight is the catabolic picture of insulin deficiency and pushes toward type 1 / ketosis-prone disease. Recorded SEPARATELY from the ADA triad, because ADA's classic symptoms are polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss — polyphagia must not be allowed to satisfy the single-random-glucose diagnostic rule.
symptoms.standard: Clinical Methods: The History, Physical, and Laboratory Examinations, 3rd ed., Ch. 'Diabetes Mellitus'
symptoms.standardVersion: Walker HK, Hall WD, Hurst JW (eds), NCBI Bookshelf NBK242
symptoms.quote: Symptoms of new onset or poor control of diabetes include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, fatigue, and vaginal Candida infections.

properties.whyItMatters: Only 'eating more while losing weight' is the insulin-deficiency combination. Eating more and gaining weight is ordinary and changes nothing.

symptoms.display: Unintentional weight loss
symptoms.whyItMatters: One of the features ADA calls most useful in determining type 1 diabetes, and part of the classic triad. Its presence tips the immediate decision toward starting insulin rather than an oral agent.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 2
symptoms.quote: The features most useful in determination of type 1 diabetes include younger age at diagnosis (<35 years) with lower BMI (<25 kg/m2), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and plasma glucose >360 mg/dL (>20 mmol/L) at presentation.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where the patient has never been weighed, the proxy options below are the only way magnitude can be recorded at all. Recording WHICH kind of evidence it was tells the reviewer how much to trust the number.

properties.whyItMatters: Only unintentional loss carries the type 1 signal. Deliberate loss on a diet or on GLP-1 therapy must not be counted toward it.
Magnitude over a stated period separates catabolic loss from ordinary fluctuation, and sets how hard to look for a competing cause (TB, HIV, malignancy) in this population.
Amount is meaningless without the interval; rapid loss over weeks is the type 1 pattern, slow loss over a year is not.
Distinguishes a documented number from an impression, which is what determines whether the figure can be used in a type-1 assessment or only as supporting history.

symptoms.display: Fatigue / unusual tiredness
symptoms.whyItMatters: Named in clinical-methods teaching and in the 4 Ts, but on its own it is nonspecific — so the decision it changes is a negative one: the form must NOT let fatigue alone count as a 'classic symptom' and thereby turn a single random glucose into a diagnosis.
symptoms.standard: Clinical Methods, Ch. 'Diabetes Mellitus'
symptoms.quote: Symptoms of new onset or poor control of diabetes include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, fatigue, and vaginal Candida infections.

symptoms.display: Blurred vision
symptoms.whyItMatters: Blurring that fluctuates with glucose is osmotic lens swelling and reverses with control — so it should NOT trigger urgent ophthalmology referral or a new spectacle prescription. Separating it from the painless progressive loss of retinopathy/maculopathy is the decision.
symptoms.standard: Clinical Methods, Ch. 'Diabetes Mellitus'
symptoms.quote: recent blurring of vision may simply indicate lens swelling and poor control

properties.whyItMatters: Fluctuating blur is treated by fixing the glucose; constant/progressive loss, sudden loss and new floaters are a different pathway. ADA also warns that any level of retinopathy or macular oedema may be asymptomatic, so a normal answer here cannot cancel retinal screening.

symptoms.display: Genital thrush, skin candidiasis or generalised itch (pruritus)
symptoms.whyItMatters: Recurrent or treatment-resistant genital candidiasis in an undiagnosed adult is a reason to check glucose at that same visit rather than treat and discharge — it is one of the few presentations where diabetes is found in an otherwise well person.
symptoms.standard: Clinical Methods, Ch. 'Diabetes Mellitus'
symptoms.quote: Symptoms of new onset or poor control of diabetes include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, fatigue, and vaginal Candida infections.

properties.whyItMatters: Candidal sites are the ones tied to glycosuria and hyperglycaemia; generalised itch without candidiasis has other causes and should not be scored as a diabetes symptom.

properties.display: Recurrent, or failed standard antifungal treatment
properties.whyItMatters: Recurrence or treatment failure is what converts a very common complaint into a reason to test for diabetes; a single responsive episode does not.

symptoms.display: Nausea and vomiting
symptoms.whyItMatters: Present in over half of DKA and uncommon in HHS, so it steers the crisis pathway; and vomiting is what makes oral rehydration impossible against ongoing osmotic loss, forcing intravenous fluids.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report (ADA/EASD/AACE/JBDS/DTS)
symptoms.quote: Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain are common in DKA (>50%) but are uncommon in HHS.

properties.display: Able to keep oral fluids down
properties.whyItMatters: Decides oral versus intravenous rehydration, which is the single most time-critical decision in a hyperglycaemic crisis.
Persistent vomiting means losses continue while intake stops; an isolated episode does not change the fluid plan.

symptoms.display: Abdominal pain
symptoms.whyItMatters: In a hyperglycaemic crisis the pain may be the acidosis itself, or it may be the precipitating illness (pancreatitis, sepsis, a surgical abdomen). Which it is decides whether the abdomen is imaged and reviewed surgically, or treated with insulin and fluids alone.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: Caution is needed with patients who present with abdominal pain because the symptoms could be either a result of the DKA or an indication of a precipitating cause of DKA, particularly in the absence of severe metabolic acidosis.

dangerSign.action: Further clinical evaluation is necessary if this complaint is not resolved with the resolution of dehydration and metabolic acidosis.

properties.display: Behaviour of the pain with treatment

options.display: Resolved as dehydration and acidosis corrected

properties.whyItMatters: The consensus makes persistence after dehydration and acidosis resolve the explicit trigger for further evaluation. This is the property the guideline itself acts on.
The consensus flags abdominal pain WITHOUT severe metabolic acidosis as the combination most likely to represent a separate precipitating cause rather than the DKA.

symptoms.display: Change in level of consciousness or cognition
symptoms.whyItMatters: Change in cognitive state marks a SEVERE crisis rather than a moderate one, which changes the level of monitoring, the airway plan and whether the patient can be managed on a general ward.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: Changes in cognitive state are usually present in patients with severe DKA and HHS.

properties.whyItMatters: Graded rather than yes/no because the guideline ties cognitive change to severity, and because the drowsy patient can no longer drink — which changes the fluid route.

symptoms.display: Deep sighing (Kussmaul) breathing, with or without acetone breath
symptoms.whyItMatters: It is the bedside evidence of metabolic acidosis. Where blood ketones and blood gases are unavailable, it is one of the few discriminators between DKA and HHS that can be obtained at the bedside, and it directs the patient to the DKA protocol.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: The respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis found in DKA is manifest by Kussmaul breathing, which consists of deep breaths with a fruity odour smell because of the presence of acetone.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: The same consensus notes that the anion gap 'may still have some utility in resource settings where ketone measurement is unavailable'. Where neither ketones nor gases exist, this physical sign plus glucose is what you have — record it deliberately, not as free text.

properties.whyItMatters: Named in the guideline description of DKA; in a setting with no ketone strips it is corroborating evidence for the ketoacidosis pathway.

symptoms.display: Previous episodes of DKA
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA requires DKA frequency, severity and cause to be recorded. Recurrent DKA with a consistent cause — most often insulin omission for cost or supply — changes the intervention from acute treatment to fixing supply, education and support, which is the only thing that stops it recurring.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 4 (Comprehensive Medical Evaluation), Table 4.1
symptoms.quote: DKA frequency, severity, and cause (if applicable)

properties.whyItMatters: Frequency is one of the three things ADA names; it is what identifies the recurrent-DKA patient who needs a supply and support intervention.
'Cause' is named explicitly by ADA. A pattern of omission is fixed differently from a pattern of infection, and 'never identified' is itself a finding that should prompt a fuller review.

symptoms.display: Burning, tingling, shooting pain or numbness in the feet
symptoms.whyItMatters: Symptom QUALITY selects the pathway: painful dysaesthesia indicates small-fibre involvement and raises the question of neuropathic pain treatment, while numbness indicates large-fibre loss of protective sensation and puts the patient into the at-risk-foot pathway with annual 10-g monofilament testing. The two need different actions.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12 (Retinopathy, Neuropathy, and Foot Care)
symptoms.quote: pain and dysesthesia (unpleasant sensations of burning and tingling)
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: ADA requires annual 10-g monofilament testing for every person with diabetes; a monofilament is cheap and reusable, and the symptom history cannot substitute for it — up to half of diabetic peripheral neuropathy is asymptomatic.

properties.whyItMatters: Splits small-fibre (pain, dysaesthesia) from large-fibre (numbness, loss of protective sensation). The first leads to pain management; the second leads to foot protection, footwear and education.
ADA says other causes of neuropathy should be considered when the clinical features are atypical. A one-limb or patchy asymmetric pattern changes the work-up rather than the diabetes treatment.

properties.display: Exposures that cause a non-diabetic neuropathy
properties.whyItMatters: ADA names these as alternative causes to consider; a positive answer changes the investigation ordered, and several of them are treatable in a way diabetic neuropathy is not.

Recorded ONLY to track response to neuropathic pain treatment over time — no diabetes-specific validated symptom score was named in the ADA section retrieved, so this must not be presented as a validated neuropathy grade.

symptoms.display: Impact of neuropathic pain on sleep, mobility and mood
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA states neuropathic pain can limit mobility and contribute to depression and social dysfunction. Impact — not intensity — is what justifies escalating to pharmacological treatment and to a mood assessment, which is a different decision from simply recording that pain exists.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: Neuropathic pain can be severe and can impact quality of life, limit mobility, and contribute to depression and social dysfunction

properties.whyItMatters: Each named domain maps to a different response: sleep and mood to treatment and screening for depression, mobility to falls and foot risk.

symptoms.display: Open ulcer, or unexplained swelling, redness or warmth of the foot
symptoms.whyItMatters: This is the guideline's own trigger for urgent referral, and it is the highest-yield single question in the whole foot history — the difference between a healed foot and an amputation.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: Individuals with any open ulceration or unexplained swelling, erythema, or increased skin temperature should be referred urgently to a foot care specialist

dangerSign.action: should be referred urgently to a foot care specialist

symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where no foot-care specialist exists, the field should still fire; the tool should record that urgent referral was indicated and to whom the patient was actually sent, rather than suppressing the flag because the service is absent.

properties.whyItMatters: Each of the first four is independently sufficient for urgent referral under the ADA wording; recording which one was seen documents why the flag fired.
ADA names exactly these items as the history to obtain; they set the patient's foot-risk category and therefore the review interval, independently of today's findings.

symptoms.display: Warm, swollen, red foot in a person with neuropathy
symptoms.whyItMatters: This specific combination is what ADA singles out for immediate offloading. Treating it as cellulitis and letting the patient keep walking destroys the joint architecture, so the decision it changes is weight-bearing, not antibiotics.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: individuals with neuropathy who present with a warm, swollen, red foot with or without a history of trauma...require total non–weight-bearing and urgent referral to a foot care specialist

dangerSign.action: require total non–weight-bearing and urgent referral to a foot care specialist

properties.whyItMatters: The ADA statement is specifically about individuals with neuropathy; the same foot in someone with intact sensation is a different differential.
Recorded precisely so that its ABSENCE is not used to dismiss the diagnosis — ADA says 'with or without a history of trauma'.

symptoms.display: Leg fatigue, calf pain on walking, or rest pain relieved by hanging the leg down
symptoms.whyItMatters: This exact symptom set is ADA's trigger for ankle–brachial index measurement. It also changes the interpretation of foot pain: ischaemic rest pain relieved by dependency is managed vascularly, neuropathic night pain is not.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: Individuals with a history of leg fatigue, claudication, and rest pain relieved with dependency...should be referred for ankle-brachial index

options.display: Calf pain on walking, relieved by rest

properties.whyItMatters: These are the three phrases the guideline itself acts on; mapping the patient's words onto them is what makes the ABI referral rule executable.

properties.display: Rest pain relieved by hanging the leg down
properties.whyItMatters: Relief on dependency is the discriminator in the ADA sentence and is what separates critical limb ischaemia from painful neuropathy, which is worse in bed for a different reason.

symptoms.display: Dizziness or fainting on standing
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA's named screening question for autonomic neuropathy. A positive answer changes antihypertensive and diuretic prescribing, triggers lying-and-standing blood pressure measurement, and changes falls advice.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: Screening can include asking about orthostatic dizziness, syncope, or dry cracked skin in the extremities.

options.display: On standing from sitting or lying

properties.whyItMatters: Only the postural pattern supports orthostatic hypotension; non-postural dizziness sends the assessment elsewhere and should not be counted as autonomic screening.
Syncope, named separately by ADA, raises the stakes to driving and occupational advice and to a cardiac assessment, not just a medication review.

symptoms.display: Dry, cracked skin of the feet or hands
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA names it as both an autonomic screening question and a sign of sudomotor dysfunction; cracked skin is a portal for the foot infection that the whole foot pathway exists to prevent, so it changes emollient and foot-care instruction.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: Signs of autonomic neuropathy include orthostatic hypotension, a resting tachycardia, or evidence of peripheral dryness or cracking of skin.

symptoms.display: Early satiety, bloating, nausea or vomiting of undigested food
symptoms.whyItMatters: Gastroparesis is a named manifestation of autonomic neuropathy, and it is the reason a patient's glucose becomes unpredictable after meals — which changes the timing of prandial insulin rather than its dose.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: resting tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, constipation, diarrhea, fecal incontinence, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, and sudomotor dysfunction

properties.whyItMatters: Vomiting undigested food hours after a meal is the feature that distinguishes delayed emptying from ordinary dyspepsia and justifies changing insulin timing rather than adding an antacid.

properties.display: Able to maintain food and fluid intake
properties.whyItMatters: Inability to maintain intake is what escalates gastroparesis from a symptom to a nutritional and hypoglycaemia risk requiring referral.

symptoms.display: Constipation, diarrhoea or faecal incontinence
symptoms.whyItMatters: These are named autonomic manifestations. Identifying them stops autonomic diarrhoea being treated repeatedly as infection, and flags the patient as autonomically involved — which is the reason to go looking for orthostatic hypotension and hypoglycaemia unawareness, both of which change acute safety decisions.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: resting tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, constipation, diarrhea, fecal incontinence, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, and sudomotor dysfunction

properties.whyItMatters: Faecal incontinence is almost never volunteered and is separately named by ADA; capturing it as an option is the only way it gets recorded at all.

symptoms.display: Erectile dysfunction or other sexual dysfunction
symptoms.whyItMatters: A named autonomic manifestation that is essentially never volunteered — asking directly is the only way it is recorded. Its presence is the prompt to look for the other autonomic features that do change acute safety (orthostatic hypotension, hypoglycaemia unawareness).
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: resting tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, constipation, diarrhea, fecal incontinence, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, and sudomotor dysfunction

symptoms.display: Incomplete bladder emptying, straining, or recurrent urinary infection
symptoms.whyItMatters: Neurogenic bladder is a named autonomic manifestation. It changes the interpretation of two other fields: it explains recurrent UTI without new hyperglycaemia, and it explains 'frequency' that is not osmotic polyuria — which would otherwise be miscounted as a classic symptom.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: resting tachycardia, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, constipation, diarrhea, fecal incontinence, erectile dysfunction, neurogenic bladder, and sudomotor dysfunction

properties.whyItMatters: These separate a retention picture from osmotic polyuria; the two lead to opposite actions (bladder assessment versus glucose testing).

symptoms.display: Hypoglycaemia episode
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA requires the hypoglycaemia history to be reviewed at every clinical encounter for anyone at risk. Frequency, severity and precipitants are what force a relaxation of the glycaemic target or a reduction in insulin or sulfonylurea — the commonest avoidable harm in diabetes care.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 6 (Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia)
symptoms.quote: History of hypoglycemia should be reviewed at every clinical encounter for all individuals at risk for hypoglycemia and evaluated as indicated.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: Where meters and strips are scarce, most episodes will never have a confirmed reading. The 'symptoms only, no reading' option keeps the episode recordable instead of lost, which matters because a level 3 event is defined by needing assistance, not by a number.

options.display: Level 1: glucose <70 mg/dL (<3.9 mmol/L) and ≥54 mg/dL (≥3.0 mmol/L)
Level 3: severe — needed someone else's help

properties.whyItMatters: ADA defines level 3 by altered mental or physical status requiring assistance for treatment — a categorically different event from a low reading, and one that mandates a change in regimen and target.
Frequency is one of the items ADA names explicitly; it is the number that drives the dose or target change.

ADA names precipitants explicitly, and each maps to a different corrective action — basal dose, meal timing, exercise carbohydrate, alcohol counselling. 'None identified' with recurrent lows is itself the signal to reduce the regimen.

options.display: Typical warning symptoms (shakiness, sweating, hunger, palpitations)

properties.whyItMatters: ADA says to record symptoms 'or lack thereof'. Losing the warning symptoms — or having only neuroglycopenic ones — is the finding that raises the glycaemic target and changes driving advice.

symptoms.display: Impaired awareness of hypoglycaemia
symptoms.whyItMatters: Loss of warning symptoms is what raises the glycaemic target, relaxes the A1C goal, and changes driving and occupational advice. It is asked as a specific question because it will not be volunteered.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 6
symptoms.quote: The Clark and Gold scores are validated questionnaires to assess impaired hypoglycemia awareness
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: ADA itself notes the validated questionnaires 'may be impractical for routine clinical use'; the two direct questions below are the guideline's own practical substitute and need no materials.

properties.display: Ever has a low glucose without feeling any symptoms
properties.whyItMatters: This is ADA's own screening question, verbatim in intent, and a yes is sufficient to change the target.

properties.display: Glucose level at which symptoms usually begin
properties.whyItMatters: ADA's second screening question. The number tracks whether awareness is recovering after targets are relaxed, which is the only way to know the intervention worked.

symptoms.display: Current infection or intercurrent illness
symptoms.whyItMatters: Infection is the most common precipitant of DKA worldwide. Finding and naming the source is the treatable half of the crisis — insulin and fluids alone will not fix it.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: Worldwide, infection is the most common precipitating factor for DKA, occurring in 14–58% of cases
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: The option list below is deliberately generic. Locally prevalent precipitants in this deployment (malaria, tuberculosis) are clinically obvious but were NOT named in any source retrieved here — a local guideline should authorise them before they are added.

properties.whyItMatters: Identifies the source, which determines the antimicrobial; a positive foot answer also crosses into the urgent foot-referral rule.

properties.display: Did the illness start before the glucose rose?
properties.whyItMatters: Establishes the illness as the precipitant rather than a consequence, which is what makes it the thing to treat alongside the metabolic derangement.

symptoms.display: Missed, reduced or interrupted diabetes treatment
symptoms.whyItMatters: Insulin omission is a major cause of DKA, and it is the one precipitant corrected by conversation, supply and support rather than by drugs. Identifying it redirects the whole intervention.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: The omission of insulin therapy, often in the setting of psychological and socioeconomic factors, is a major cause of DKA
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: The consensus explicitly attributes omission to socioeconomic as well as psychological factors. Cost, stockout and cold-chain failure need to be first-class options, not 'other', or the reason will never be recorded and never fixed.

properties.whyItMatters: Insulin omission specifically is what the consensus links to DKA; missing an oral agent carries different urgency.
Each reason has a different and specific remedy. Without this field the note records 'non-adherence' and nothing changes.
Duration of insulin interruption is what makes ketoacidosis plausible within the hours-to-days window the consensus describes for DKA onset.

symptoms.display: New or recently changed medication affecting glucose
symptoms.whyItMatters: Each of these drugs has a documented and specific action attached: an SGLT2 inhibitor must be stopped on admission and makes DKA possible at a normal glucose; a glucocorticoid predicts sustained hyperglycaemia that needs anticipatory dose change rather than reactive correction.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: Glucocorticoids may precipitate acute and sustained hyperglycaemia by countering insulin action

properties.whyItMatters: SGLT2 inhibitor selects the euglycaemic-DKA rule; glucocorticoid selects anticipatory insulin adjustment; checkpoint inhibitor raises new-onset autoimmune diabetes (reported in ~1–2% of recipients), which is an insulin-requiring diagnosis rather than a type 2 one.
Recency is what makes the drug a plausible precipitant of this presentation rather than background therapy.

symptoms.display: PERTINENT NEGATIVE — classic osmotic symptoms specifically denied
symptoms.whyItMatters: The single most decision-changing negative in the form. Without classic symptoms, one random glucose ≥200 mg/dL CANNOT diagnose diabetes; a second abnormal result is required. Recording the denial is what stops a one-off reading becoming a lifelong diagnosis and a lifelong prescription.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 2
symptoms.quote: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia, diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests which may be obtained at the same time...or the same test at two different time points.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: This negative COSTS money — it mandates a second test. That is exactly why it must be recorded deliberately rather than inferred from an empty field, so the recall is planned and not silently skipped.

properties.display: Were these symptoms specifically asked about?
properties.whyItMatters: A negative is only usable if it was actually asked. 'Denied' and 'not documented' must never collapse into the same value, or the confirmatory-test rule will be applied to guesses.
Only the first three are ADA's classic triad. Denying polyphagia or blurred vision does not affect the diagnostic rule, and the form must be able to tell the difference.

symptoms.display: PERTINENT NEGATIVE — no nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain
symptoms.whyItMatters: These occur in over half of DKA and are uncommon in HHS. In a hyperosmolar, markedly hyperglycaemic patient their explicit absence shifts the working diagnosis toward HHS, which has a different fluid and insulin protocol. It does NOT exclude DKA, and the form must never let it be used to skip a ketone measurement.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: Nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain are common in DKA (>50%) but are uncommon in HHS.

properties.whyItMatters: Distinguishes an actual denial from an undocumented field before the tool lets the answer shift a differential.

symptoms.display: PERTINENT NEGATIVE — glucose NOT markedly raised in a patient with possible ketoacidosis
symptoms.whyItMatters: About 10% of DKA is euglycaemic, and in reported series 35% and 71% of SGLT2-inhibitor-associated DKA presented at glucose below the usual thresholds. Recording 'glucose was not high' TOGETHER with SGLT2 inhibitor use is what stops a normal glucose being read as 'not DKA' and a ketone test being skipped.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: Approximately 10% of patients with DKA present with euglycaemic DKA, which is defined as plasma glucose levels <11.1 mmol/l (200 mg/dl) in the presence of ketosis and metabolic acidosis criteria of DKA.
symptoms.resourceLimitedNote: The consensus recommends direct measurement of β-hydroxybutyrate and warns that urine ketone testing can underestimate ketonaemia early in DKA. Where only urine strips exist, a negative or trace strip in a symptomatic patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor must not close the case.

properties.whyItMatters: This is the combination that produces euglycaemic DKA; the consensus also states SGLT2 inhibitors should be stopped on admission, so a yes triggers a drug action as well as a test.

Determines how much weight the negative can bear. The consensus notes urine testing lags early in DKA, and that the anion gap retains utility 'in resource settings where ketone measurement is unavailable'.

symptoms.display: PERTINENT NEGATIVE — no foot symptoms reported
symptoms.whyItMatters: Up to half of diabetic peripheral neuropathy is asymptomatic. So a denial of symptoms must NOT be allowed to satisfy the annual neuropathy assessment — the form should record the negative and still require the 10-g monofilament plus pinprick or vibration examination.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: Up to 50% of diabetic peripheral neuropathy may be asymptomatic.

properties.display: Was the foot examination performed anyway?
properties.whyItMatters: This is the whole point of the field: it makes visible the case where a symptom denial was allowed to substitute for the examination, which is how at-risk feet are missed.

symptoms.display: PERTINENT NEGATIVE — vision reported as normal
symptoms.whyItMatters: Any level of retinopathy or macular oedema may be asymptomatic. Recording 'vision normal' must not cancel or defer the retinal screening requirement — the negative exists to be overridden, and the form should say so.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 12
symptoms.quote: individuals with any level of diabetic retinopathy or macular edema may be asymptomatic

properties.whyItMatters: Pairs the negative with the only thing that can actually exclude retinopathy, and makes 'not available at this site' a recordable, referable state rather than a silent gap.

symptoms.display: PERTINENT NEGATIVE — no hypoglycaemia episodes since last review
symptoms.whyItMatters: ADA requires the hypoglycaemia history at every encounter and names 'symptoms (or lack thereof)' as part of what to record. A documented absence of episodes is what justifies tightening a glycaemic target; an undocumented field is not the same thing and should not be treated as one.
symptoms.standard: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Section 6
symptoms.quote: hypoglycemic event frequency, severity, precipitants, symptoms (or lack thereof), and approach to treatment

properties.display: Was glucose monitoring available during the period?
properties.whyItMatters: A 'no episodes' answer from someone with no meter is a statement about testing, not about glucose. Without this field the negative is misleading in exactly the settings where it is most often given.

symptoms.display: PERTINENT NEGATIVE — insulin/oral therapy confirmed taken as prescribed
symptoms.whyItMatters: Omission is a major cause of DKA. Explicitly excluding it redirects the search for a precipitant toward infection and the other acute causes, and it documents that the drug and supply history was actually taken rather than assumed.
symptoms.standard: Hyperglycaemic crises in adults with diabetes: a consensus report
symptoms.quote: Other acute conditions that may precipitate DKA include stroke, alcohol and substance use, pancreatitis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction and trauma

properties.whyItMatters: An unverified 'taking it as prescribed' is the answer most likely to be wrong in exactly the patients who present in crisis; recording how it was established prevents the negative from closing the line of enquiry prematurely.

mnemonicFindings.expansion: Polyuria (urinating a lot), Polydipsia (drinking a lot), Polyphagia (eating a lot), Weight loss for no apparent reason, Pruritus (itchy rash)
mnemonicFindings.note: This is the ONLY source I could retrieve that states a '5 Ps' list, and it is a private hospital's patient-education page, not a clinical guideline. Two cautions before this is shown to clinicians: (1) 'weight loss' is not a P, so the mnemonic is internally inconsistent and people will mis-recall it; (2) no ADA, WHO, NICE or consensus document I retrieved uses a 5 Ps framing at all — ADA's own phrase is 'classic hyperglycemic symptoms (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss)'. Recommendation: key the diagnostic logic to the ADA triad, and if the 5 Ps are shown at all, label them as a teaching aid, not guideline content.

Appeared repeatedly across search results (Healthline, nursing.com, university extension pages) but I did NOT retrieve any of those pages, so I am recording it as unsourced. Note the clinically important divergence: the widely taught 3 Ps end in polyphagia, whereas ADA's classic triad ends in unexplained weight loss. Since it is the ADA triad — not polyphagia — that licenses diagnosis from a single random glucose, a tool that treats '3 Ps satisfied' as 'classic symptoms present' would be wrong.

mnemonicFindings.expansion: NOT SOURCED — no expansion could be verified
mnemonicFindings.note: I could NOT source a '3 Ws' mnemonic for diabetes in any form. Five searches (including nursing-education, medical-student and Uganda-specific framings, and candidate expansions built around weeing / water / weight loss / wasting / weakness) returned nothing. It may be a local or institutional teaching aid. Do not ship it. The closest verifiable mnemonic of that shape is Diabetes UK's 4 Ts, below.

mnemonicFindings.expansion: Toilet — 'going to the toilet a lot, bed-wetting by a previously dry child or heavier nappies in babies'; Thirsty — 'being really thirsty and not being able to quench the thirst'; Tired — 'feeling more tired than usual'; Thinner — 'losing weight or looking thinner than usual'
mnemonicFindings.note: Verified verbatim. This is a public-awareness campaign aimed at parents and at earlier recognition of type 1 diabetes in children, not a clinical guideline — so it is good source material for the WORDING of symptom questions (especially the bed-wetting and unquenchable-thirst phrasings, which I have used in the property options above) but it should not be cited as the basis of a diagnostic rule. The page I fetched did not name DKA.

mnemonicFindings.expansion: Age (younger, <35 suggests type 1); Autoimmunity (personal or family history of autoimmune disease); Body habitus (lower BMI); Background (family history); Control (inability to reach glycaemic goals on non-insulin therapy); Comorbidities (e.g. immune checkpoint inhibitor exposure)
mnemonicFindings.note: Named as a clinical tool in ADA Standards of Care Section 2 for distinguishing type 1 from type 2 diabetes in adults. IMPORTANT: the retrieval returned the six letters in paraphrase, not as a verbatim block quote, so the exact expansion of each letter should be checked against the published PDF before it is displayed to clinicians. The surrounding ADA text I did verify verbatim is more directly useful for the tool anyway: 'The features most useful in determination of type 1 diabetes include younger age at diagnosis (<35 years) with lower BMI (<25 kg/m2), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and plasma glucose >360 mg/dL (>20 mmol/L) at presentation', and 'Less discriminatory features include non-White ethnicity, family history, longer duration and milder severity of symptoms prior to presentation, features of metabolic syndrome, and absence of a family history of autoimmunity.'

mnemonicFindings.mnemonic: ADA 'classic symptoms' (not a mnemonic, but the phrase the diagnostic rule actually turns on)
mnemonicFindings.expansion: Polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss
mnemonicFindings.note: Verified verbatim: 'classic hyperglycemic symptoms (e.g., polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss)'. This — not the 3 Ps and not the 5 Ps — is the set the tool should evaluate when deciding whether a single random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L) can stand as a diagnosis.

unverifiable: '3 Ws' mnemonic — could not be sourced at all, in any expansion. Not shipped, and should not be added without a named local source.
'5 Ps' — sourced only to a private hospital patient-education page (emc.id), not to any guideline. Treat as a teaching aid only.
'3 Ps' — I did not retrieve any page stating it; recorded from search-result summaries only.

URGENT-ACTION WORDING FOR DKA/HHS SYMPTOMS. This is the most important gap. I could NOT retrieve, from the 2024 hyperglycaemic crises consensus, any explicit statement instructing urgent action for altered consciousness, Kussmaul breathing, persistent vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down; the prevention section I fetched says only that patients 'need to review the appropriate glucose and ketone monitoring and when to call for assistance' without naming the symptoms. Following the rule that dangerSign is set only where the guideline itself demands urgent action, I have left these WITHOUT danger-sign flags. That is a deliberate under-flagging and a clinician reviewer must source proper red-flag wording (e.g. from JBDS inpatient guidance or a local emergency protocol) before this form is used on acutely unwell patients.
Sick-day rules generally — no verbatim guidance retrieved on not omitting insulin during illness, increasing monitoring frequency, or thresholds for seeking help.

WHO HEARTS-D (diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes) — every route to the PDF returned HTTP 403. No WHO wording is verified anywhere in this output, including anything about diagnosis where laboratory resources are limited.

NICE NG17 (type 1 diabetes in adults) — nice.org.uk returned HTTP 403. The NICE clinical criteria for diagnosing type 1 on clinical grounds (ketosis, rapid weight loss, age below 50, BMI below 25, personal/family autoimmune history) and the 'do not discount type 1 if BMI ≥25 or age ≥50' caution are NOT verified here; the type 1 discriminators above come solely from ADA.
Uganda Ministry of Health / Uganda Clinical Guidelines NCD content — not located. No locally authorised danger signs, referral thresholds or drug-availability constraints are reflected.

Malaria and tuberculosis as intercurrent precipitants of hyperglycaemic crisis in this deployment — clinically obvious but named in NO source I retrieved. I left them out of the option list deliberately; a local guideline should authorise them.

VALIDATED SYMPTOM SEVERITY INSTRUMENTS. Only the Clarke and Gold scores (hypoglycaemia awareness) were verified, and ADA itself notes they 'may be impractical for routine clinical use'. I searched ADA Section 12 specifically and it named NO validated instrument — not MNSI, DN4, NTSS-6, Toronto Clinical Neuropathy Score, Utah Early Neuropathy Scale, Gastroparesis Cardinal Symptom Index, IIEF-5, or the Walking Impairment Questionnaire. The 0–10 pain rating I proposed is explicitly labelled as a tracking aid, not a validated grade. Do not add scored instruments to this form without sourcing them.

Nocturia. The polyuria threshold (>3 L per 24 h, or 50 mL/kg per 24 h) is verified from StatPearls. The distinction between polyuria and urinary frequency, and a definition of nocturia, were NOT returned by that fetch — I used them because they are the basis of the volume-vs-frequency property, but the wording is mine, not a source's.
Bed-wetting in a previously dry child comes from a Diabetes UK awareness campaign, not a clinical guideline.
Blurred vision laterality (one eye vs both) — no source retrieved; property omitted for that reason.

Urgent-referral wording for symptomatic sudden visual loss, floaters, vitreous haemorrhage or retinal detachment — not retrieved. ADA Section 12 gave only 'If diabetic retinopathy is evident on screening, prompt referral to an ophthalmologist is recommended', which is about a screening finding, not a presenting symptom. No danger sign set on visual symptoms as a result.

Localised versus generalised abdominal pain as a discriminator for a surgical precipitant in DKA — not guideline-specified. The consensus says only that the pain 'could be either a result of the DKA or an indication of a precipitating cause'.

Gastroparesis producing post-meal hypoglycaemia followed by late hyperglycaemia, and therefore changing prandial insulin TIMING — this mechanism is not stated in any source I retrieved; ADA Section 12 only names gastroparesis in a list of autonomic manifestations. The property was softened accordingly.
'Poor wound healing' as a classic presenting symptom — not found in the retrieved text of Clinical Methods or StatPearls. Folded into the foot pathway rather than proposed as its own classic symptom.

ADA Section 4 Table 4.1 lines came back truncated mid-sentence (e.g. 'History of diabetes complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy,'). The items are real but the full wording of that table is not verified.

GUIDELINE VERSION DRIFT. Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026 was published in December 2025 and is the current edition, but I could not retrieve its full text (diabetesjournals.org returned 403; the PMC id I tried was the disclosures document). Section 2 quotes above are from the 2025 edition; Sections 4, 6 and 12 are from the 2024 edition, retrieved via PMC. All of these must be re-checked against the 2026 text before clinical deployment, and the standardVersion fields updated.

Nephropathy has no symptom entry at all. It is silent until advanced, so there is no symptom that changes a decision — the decision is driven by albuminuria and eGFR testing, which is out of scope for a symptom form. Flagging it so the omission is understood as deliberate.

Cardiovascular symptoms (chest pain, breathlessness) and the phenomenon of silent myocardial ischaemia in diabetes are not covered here; the crises consensus names myocardial infarction only as a DKA precipitant. A cardiovascular symptom set needs its own sourcing pass.

Unit handling: mg/dL and mmol/L figures are reproduced exactly as the guidelines state them. I did not independently recompute any conversion, and the tool must not display a converted value that no source stated.

audit.reason: PMC11635041 is genuinely '2. Diagnosis and Classification of Diabetes: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2025', Diabetes Care 48(Suppl 1):S27–S49, as claimed. Table 2.1 verbatim: 'In an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis, a random plasma glucose ≥200 mg/dL (≥11.1 mmol/L).' Classic symptoms verbatim: 'polyuria, polydipsia, and unexplained weight loss'. Rec 2.1b verbatim: 'In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycemia (e.g., hyperglycemic crises), diagnosis requires confirmatory testing.' The decision named is real and correctly attributed.
audit.correction: Two fixes. (1) The proposer's 'a second abnormal test is required' invites a return-visit UI. ADA's footnote is narrower: 'diagnosis requires two abnormal results from different tests which may be obtained at the same time (e.g., A1C and FPG), or the same test at two different time points.' A same-visit A1C satisfies it — important where follow-up is unreliable. (2) The props onset_speed and duration have no decision attached in Section 2. onset_speed is defensible but from a different source (PMC11343900: DKA 'hours to a few days', HHS 'days or weeks'); duration is unjustified — drop it or cite it. Also cite the current edition: PMC12690183 (2026, Diabetes Care 49 Suppl 1) carries word-for-word identical language.

audit.reason: Half confirmed, half unsupported. The triad membership is verbatim in the cited Section 2. But the second decision — 'whether the patient can still drink enough to replace osmotic losses decides between oral rehydration and immediate intravenous fluids' — is in neither cited nor adjacent source. ADA Section 2 is a diagnosis-and-classification document containing no fluid recommendations at all. I grepped the 2024 hyperglycaemic crises report (PMC11343900) for 'oral rehydration', 'oral fluid' and 'drink': zero hits in 137k characters. That report treats DKA and HHS with intravenous fluids throughout ('The management of DKA and HHS includes the administration of intravenous fluids, insulin and electrolytes'). The prop oral_intake_maintained is one of only two props and rests entirely on this unsourced claim.
audit.correction: The rationale is clinically defensible but cited to the wrong document. It is quotable from ADA Standards of Care 2026 Section 6 (PMC12690178), which does contemplate outpatient management of mild DKA with 'noncaloric hydration' and subcutaneous insulin, and states: 'individuals should seek immediate medical attention if they are unable to tolerate oral hydration, they experience ongoing emesis, blood glucose levels and/or ketone levels do not improve with insulin administration, altered mental status is present, or any signs of worsening illness occur.' Re-cite oral_intake_maintained there, or delete it.

audit.reason: NBK242 verbatim: 'Symptoms of new onset or poor control of diabetes include polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss, fatigue, and vaginal Candida infections.' The chapter is genuinely Clinical Methods 3rd ed., Ch. 136 'Diabetes Mellitus'. The operative decision — keep polyphagia out of the set that satisfies ADA's single-random-glucose rule — is directly supported, since ADA's classic list is only polyuria, polydipsia and unexplained weight loss. This is a good safety-motivated separation.
audit.correction: One sentence of the rationale is contradicted by the proposer's own other source. 'Eating more while losing weight... pushes toward type 1 / ketosis-prone disease' is not in NBK242 and is undercut by ADA Section 2, which names the useful type 1 discriminators as 'younger age at diagnosis (<35 years) with lower BMI (<25 kg/m2), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and plasma glucose >360 mg/dL' — polyphagia is absent — and then says explicitly: 'Other features classically associated with type 1 diabetes, such as ketosis without acidosis, osmotic symptoms, family history, or a history of autoimmune diseases, are weak discriminators.' Drop the type-1 claim; keep the field. Chapter author is Mark E. Molitch; Walker/Hall/Hurst are the book editors.

audit.reason: Verbatim in the cited Section 2: 'The features most useful in determination of type 1 diabetes include younger age at diagnosis (<35 years) with lower BMI (<25 kg/m2), unintentional weight loss, ketoacidosis, and plasma glucose >360 mg/dL (>20 mmol/L) at presentation.' It is also verbatim a member of the classic triad. Both halves of the attribution hold.
audit.correction: 'Its presence tips the immediate decision toward starting insulin rather than an oral agent' is not stated in Section 2 — that is Section 9 (Pharmacologic Approaches) territory and needs its own citation. Note also ADA's Fig. 2.1 caveat that would govern this field: 'No single clinical feature confirms type 1 diabetes in isolation,' and the flowchart is 'based on data from White European populations' — a material limitation for a Ugandan deployment. The props amount, period and evidence_type have no threshold anywhere in the source; they are reasonable but are the proposer's design choice, not the guideline's.

audit.reason: Verbatim in NBK242's symptom list. Independently corroborated by the 4 Ts page I fetched (diabetes.org.uk), which gives 'Tired — feeling more tired than usual'.
